subsubtopic: CRITERIA ESTABLISHED WITH RESPECT TO INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance who spoke yesterday to a luncheon meeting of the Canadian Club in Montreal and indicated that it was the policy of the Government of Canada to, and I quote:
-encourage the movement of productive resources from those industrial activities with diminishing prospects to strong and potentially strong industries and subsectors.
I gather that this is the beginning of the much heralded, long awaited industrial strategy the government has been talking about for so long. Can the Minister of Finance tell the House of Commons, since he has spoken of industries with diminishing prospects, just what criteria the government has established, and will he identify those sectors of Canadian industry that the government considers to have diminishing prospects?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: CRITERIA ESTABLISHED WITH RESPECT TO INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the budget speech I think I stated that there was bound to be, in a dynamic economy, changes in the composition of the labour force, and that certain industries would have to adjust to changing conditions. It seems to me that it is essential to the future strength of the Canadian economy that we take advantage of strong sectors and, where necessary, assist weaker sectors to adjust, not necessarily to go out of business but to adjust to new products and new lines of activity. It seems to me that unless we take account of that particular problem, the over-all strength of the economy will be weakened.
I would just add, in conclusion, that the adjustment program announced by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Employment and Immigration, addresses the question of adjustment and has adopted the approach of designating certain communities that might be eligible for particular adjustment assistance. I am not aware of the extent to which that process of designation has been implemented to the present time.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: CRITERIA ESTABLISHED WITH RESPECT TO INDUSTRY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we have no hit list. I believe the Leader of the Opposition ought not to take a destructive and despairing attitude about this approach. speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. It also concerns his speech to the Montreal business establishment which he said was so well received. Since wages have fallen behind in each of the past three years as a percentage of the GNP while at the same time profits, dividends and other forms of unearned income have actually gone up as a percentage of the GNP, why did the minister single out ordinary workers as the people who would have to bear this burden? Instead of growing in the last number of years, productivity in Canada has declined. I want to add that if we expect to have a higher standard of living, the economy as a whole has to produce more in order that we may enjoy that better standard of living. It is a disservice to everybody to put our heads in the sand and ignore the fact that over the past number of years output per person in the labour force has decreased and, unless we turn that around, we have very little prospect of enjoying the rising standards of living which we had in the earlier period. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. STEVENS-MASSEY-FERGUSON REFINANCING-ALLEGED MISLEADING STATEMENT OF MR. GRAY
speechtext:
On Thursday last the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) raised a question of privilege alleging that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) misled the House on February 6, 1981, and moved a motion to refer the matter to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
The hon. member's complaint flows from a question put to the minister during Oral Question Period on February 6 in which he inquired of the minister if he had a statement to make with respect to the negotiations involving his department and Massey-Ferguson. The minister replied that the matter was under review.
The hon. member alleges that the minister misled the House in his answer because, in his view, "clearly the matter was settled". In support of his arguments, the hon. member for York-Peel mentioned that the relevant cabinet meeting had been held on the previous day. He further alleges that this decision having been made, the minister chose not to inform the House, stating that it was still "under active review."
In his remarks on Thursday last, the minister indicated that he had no statement to make at the time the question was posed to him by the hon. member since the final decision was not taken until after the question period. The particular point at issue at this time is whether there exists a prima facie case of privilege upon which a motion can be entertained.
Point of Order-Mr. W. Baker
I have reviewed with care the arguments presented by all hon. members who participated in the discussions on Thursday last in order to determine precisely if a prima facie case of privilege had been established.
It seems to me that we have before us a series of facts the interpretation of which is disputed by two hon. members. Hon. members are aware of Citation No. 19(1) in Beauchesne's fifth edition which reads as follows:
A dispute arising between two members, as to allegations of facts, does not fulfil the conditions of parliamentary privilege.
I also draw to the attention of the House Citation No. 322 which reflects a long-standing practice of this House that statements made by members in this House must be accepted.
I therefore find, in this instance, that a prima facie case of privilege has not been established.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I gave you notice, I think last Thursday, of a question of privilege on a matter which affects my rights as a member of the House, and in connection with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) and his Canada community development program. Under that program the amount of $2,741,000 was allotted to the federal district of St. John's West, my district, for this year. A local advisory board was appointed to advise me, the minister and his officials, on what projects should go ahead. There were 110 projects submitted by groups throughout St. John's West. There were 43 projects approved which used up the moneys allotted. The local advisory board and the departmental officials gave a priority rating to all projects, using a scale of nine. So, these were the projects that had the highest priority. That was all done last fall. There were 67 projects which were not funded.
One of these projects was a recreation project at Mount Carmel, a community in my district, 1468 MA 2. That project had a score of .23 out of nine points. It ranked ninety-ninth of the 110 projects. Of the 67 projects not funded it ranked fifty-sixth in order of priority. The community of Mount Carmel already had a project awarded for the building of a wharf and repairing of a fisheries facility for the amount of $65,000.
The minister's office contacted me in January to ask whether I would agree to an additional $25,000 being awarded for this Mount Carmel project. I said I would look into the matter. The minister's office said he had an additional $25,000 that he could award for this project in St. John's West. I looked into the records. It just happened to be kicking around, that extra $25,000. 1 looked into this, and when I discovered that this project ranked ninety-ninth in priority of 110 projects, I did not give my consent.
I went outside Canada on a trip, and just before I got back the provincial Liberal member of the House of Assembly for the provincial district of St. Mary's-The Capes, which lies in the district of St. John's West, had made a public announcement that this project in Mount Carmel, MA 2, was going to be funded with $25,000. It was not announced by the minister's department. It was not announced by the member. The impression given to the people of St. John's West was that I had lost my senses and was misapplying public funds to fund the project that ranked ninety-ninth out of 110 projects submitted in my district.
This project did not warrant any funds being spent on it. I quote to you the guidelines of the minister's department in his letter of July 30, 1980, when he announced the program. On page 2 he set out that the applicants for these projects had to show, and 1 quote:
-an intention to follow a hiring plan aimed at the redressing of imbalances in employment opportunities for women, youth, native people and physically disabled persons-
These had to be factors in assessing proposals for funding.
The officials of the minister's department threw out this Mount Carmel project, on the grounds that it did not meet these guidelines, that it did not meet the affirmative action guidelines of the minister's program, giving two reasons for rejecting it:
i)	it is not supportive of the affirmative action principles laid out in the intentions of the program.
ii)	it only marginally meets the federal-provincial requirements (recreation).
But the Liberal provincial member for the district contacted the office of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Romp-key), who is the cabinet minister from Newfoundland, and that minister apparently contacted the minister responsible and persuaded him that for political reasons this project for Mount Carmel, sponsored by two Liberal co-workers, two Liberal campaign workers for the Liberal member, Mr. Hancock-who will be the ex-Liberal member when the next provincial election is called-convinced the minister to ignore the guidelines of the program and to misspend public moneys on this project in Mount Carmel.
In the provincial district of St. Mary's-The Capes there were 21 other projects which were not funded but scored higher in priority than this Mount Carmel project.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: My goodness.

North Harbour, St. Vincent's, O'Donnells, Gaskier's, St. Mary's, Branch, Point La Haye, Admiral's Cove, St. Bride's, Mitchell's Brook, Colinet, St. Stephen's, Harricott, Patrick's Cove and Mall Bay: all were, in order of priority, ahead of Mount Carmel. They were all in Mr. Hancock's district. He is stuck with them all. He turned his back on them. He ignored their greater priority, and he tried to favour his Liberal friends in Mount Carmel when the community already had a project.
Shame!

I will debate that gentleman, Madam Speaker. I am going to debate him in all these communities. If he shows his face in any of them in the future, he will need a bodyguard, I can assure you, for turning his back on his own constituents and favouring his Liberal friends in that community.
I referred to Hansard for June 4, 1980. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) asked the minister a question because he thought the minister's guidelines with reference to this program were unconstitutional. As reported at page 1476 of Hansard, the minister said:
We, as a government, have felt that the best source of advice as to local priorities in the various regions of Canada is members of Parliament.
He said Members of Parliament, not members of the house of assembly, not Liberal members of the house of assembly, but Members of Parliament. He went on to say:
-1 happened to conclude that Member of Parliament are the best sources of advice on our regional priorities.
Then our critic in this area, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) wrote the minister on November 4, 1980,
February 24, 1981

expressing his concern about how priorities were to be decided.
I am sorry, he wrote on August 18, and received a letter from the minister on November 4, 1980, which stated:
I propose to seek this advice from provincial governments, and from the staff of the commission. It is essential, in my view, that advice and judgment on local priorities be sought from the local level as well. In this context an important and valued source of perspective is the Member of Parliament elected to represent that area.
I do not want to take too much time on this, Madam Speaker. It was a political axe job by the Minister of Employment and Immigration who is unworthy of that office, in my view. He has approved a government program in a district where there is a local advisory board chaired by Mr. Walter Manning of St. Bride's with other members from the federal district of St. John's West. This is a district in which I have never interfered with the recommendations of the local advisory boards. They are asked to advise on local conditions and, I believe, their advice should be accepted. A project which rated 99th out of 110 received an award of $25,000 which was not in the program in the first place. It is additional money which the minister conjured up from somewhere, money that was not distributed across Canada as it was supposed to be. It was given to a project that scored .23 out of 9 points.
If I did not have this opportunity to bring the matter to your attention today, Madam Speaker, if I had not written to every newspaper in Newfoundland about it, if I had not written to every community that is involved in it, people might have thought that I had lent myself to this kind of prostitution in the spending of public funds for political purposes. But I have written, Madam Speaker, and I am going to tell every household in St. Mary's-The Capes and St. John's West just how serious the government is about unemployment and creating jobs and how they administer their programs without political favouritism and political interference. Every household in St. John's West will understand perfectly the minister's idea of the way he should carry out his public duties. They will know that because a Liberal member of the house of assembly has two Liberal friends who applied for a project, although it does not deserve public funds, and although the community already has a fishery project, an economic development project recommended by the local advisory board, the minister approves the spending of money on a program against the recommendation of his officials, against the recommendation of the local advisory board and without the concurrence of the hon. member.
I submit that this is a breach of my privileges as a member, Madam Speaker. It is disgraceful conduct on the part of the minister. It is a breach of my privileges as a member, and if you will find a prima facie case, Madam Speaker, I will move the requisite motion to have this sent to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections to which this gentleman should go to have his peers determine his fate. I have no doubt that if his peers do that impartially and justly he will be out of here within a fortnight.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lloyd Axworthy (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration

The hon. member indicated that he intends to provide his constituents with some information about this case. I hope that he will provide some additional information about the case to make sure that they have all the facts. He has been known, from time to time, to neglect giving all the information that is required.
The first thing the constituents of St. John's West should know is that this is a program of direct employment creation. It is a program which was cancelled by the hon. member when he was a minister and a member of the previous government. All of a sudden he is standing here crying great crocodile tears and saying that the poor people of St. John's West are being denied the privilege, that his government denied to every single community across Canada when they cancelled every employment creation program. Furthermore, they totally denied the right of a Member of Parliament to any consultation whatsoever when, under a similar program, they cancelled the local advisory boards.
What kind of hypocrisy is this when the hon. member will stand here and claim the rights of democracy are being denied when he and his government have denied those very rights to every member of this House? On those grounds, every member of the House could claim a breach of privilege by the hon. member opposite and the government of which he was a member.
That is not true.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: Furthermore, Madam Speaker, I find it somewhat surprising that the hon. member for St. John's West should take umbrage at the government being prepared to give more money to his constituency and at the fact that in the reallocation we were giving priorities to communities which had heavy unemployment and we were prepared to assign money. He is saying, "It was not my priority." Let me remind the hon. member that under the project in question an application was sent out. We told them and the Members of Parliament that it was not acceptable under our terms. The project was redrafted to contain new proposals. Hear, hear!

Obviously the hon. member is not of the same mentality. In the tradition of fair play, we contacted the hon. member's office and said, "Here is a reapplication for a

project. Would you give us your opinion of it?". The hon. member said, "I would be glad to. Send me the project." Members of my office staff called his office several times over the succeeding four weeks only to find out that he was off gallivanting in South Africa-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
If the constituents of the hon. member want the true facts, they should ask, "Where was he when he should have been doing his constituency work?" He was off in South Africa. It is not for me to judge why he was in South Africa: he has a right to go anywhere he wants. But if he is so preoccupied with and concerned about his constituency responsibilities, he should have given some advice to his staff before leaving so that they could have made a recommendation. He was not back in his office until February 1, and the final date for projects was February 2.
I submit, Madam Speaker, that the hon. member feels some guilt about not fulfilling his responsibilities and not looking after his constituency as he should have been doing at that time. That is why we gave approval, based upon the recommendation of a regional minister who was doing his duty and covering for the hon. member for St. John's West who was somewhere else.
I would like to see the report that the hon. member will give to his constituents. If they knew the true facts, I do not think the hon. member for St. John's West would be around this House very much longer.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) rising on the same question of privilege?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Yes, very briefly, Madam Speaker. The point raised by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) was that there has been a breach by this minister of the undertaking he gave on June 4, 1980, when he indicated:
-I happened to conclude that members of Parliament are the best sources of advice on our regional priorities.
That was the policy set down by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) on June 4, 1980. The substance of the question of privilege raised by my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West, is that that clear guideline, publicly given, was departed from in this case. That is one matter which Your Honour will have to judge, but there is now an even more interesting question raised by the very anxious and nervous Minister of Employment and Immigration. It concerns his claim in the House today that a proposal which had been rejected, had been judged to stand ninety-ninth out of 110 projects. The proponents of that proposal were asked to submit their proposal again. They were asked to rewrite it and were given a second chance at having a proposal approved which had been rejected on its merits.
That raises questions as to whether the other 16 applicants who had ranked below this particular project in St. John's West were also invited to rewrite their submissions, or whether they did not have the appropriate political colouration to have this minister ask them to try again so that they might squeeze their way into the established guidelines. That is another question to be looked at.
What we are dealing with here, Madam Speaker, are two very important matters. They require a great deal of levity from the other side. One has to do with whether the word of the Minister of Employment and Immigration can be believed. He said one thing on June 4, 1980, then he acted in another way. That is one question on which your Honour will have to judge.
The other very important question has to do with the propriety of departure from guidelines in particular instances where the minister, or his political party, happen to be involved. We have an admission from the minister that he went back to these Liberal proponents of a Liberal project and asked them to rewrite their application, after the deadlines had passed and after the opportunity had passed for everyone else, in a way which might make it the expenditure of public funds acceptable. It is very important to know whether that has been a broadly practised procedure, whether everyone is asked to rewrite their applications, or whether that privilege is extended simply to friends of the minister and to political friends of the Liberal Party whose proposals are rejected on their merits but who are then asked to rewrite their proposals so they can become eligible for $25,000 of new-found public money.
What is at issue here is whether the same standards apply to everyone. It is clear from what the minister has said that the same standards do not apply to everyone. It is clear that there is one standard applied to Liberals and a different standard applied to other more responsible citizens in the country.
There is also the question as to whether or not there has been a departure by the minister from his solemn word in this House in a way that constitutes a question of privilege. Those, Madam Speaker, are both matters upon which you will have to judge.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Judging from the discussion until now, it appears to me to be a complaint and a difference of opinion as to how the government reaches its decisions.
I will not hear too many members. I see the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) is rising. I think the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) mentioned him in his question of privilege. I would like the hon. member for Calgary West to be very brief in his remarks. I will recognize also the Hon. Minister for National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey). After that, I will determine whether or not to allow any further interventions on this question.

speechtext: Africa!

speechtext: Third, the hon. member for St. John's West indicated that it was officials who had ranked this particular project and judged it. speechtext: That explains it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue

Fourth, the member for St. John's West has accused us of cutting off spending to Newfoundland. He said that this government is deliberately cutting off spending to Newfoundland for some reason or other. According to him, we are doing that for some nefarious reason. He said we are so stupid as to cut off spending to Newfoundland, in spite of the fact that the people of Newfoundland elected five Liberals. He is making that accusation. He has accused me particularly of interfering in a project called synchrolift. Some members of the House perhaps do not know what synchrolift is, but I have been accused of cutting off that project.
However, here I am accused of helping to allocate additional funds to the member's riding. The hon. member has to make up his mind. Does the hon. member want more funds for Newfoundland or does he not? Does he want more funds for St. John's West or does he not? The hon. member has to make up his mind. If he does not want funds going to St. John's West today, then he should quite clearly say to the people of St. John's West, "I do not want any more money going into St. John's West". We will not follow that advice, but he should say it if that is what he thinks.
This is a matter, Madam Speaker, on which you will have to judge, and clearly I think you will judge that there is no
Privilege-Mr. Crosbie
question of privilege and that the Minister of Employment and Immigration acted properly in the interests of Newfoundland and Labrador, and particularly in the interest of the people of St. John's West.
Hear, hear!

Madam Speaker, I rise on this question of privilege because the letters I wrote on August 18 were mentioned by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). Those letters quoted an excerpt of Hansard for June 4. At that time the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) rose in this House to ask the minister if his guidelines for spending money in this fashion were legal. The minister did agree to consult the law officers at the Table. We do not know whether that consultation took place.
The issue being raised here today is sometimes obfuscated with rhetoric, but it is a question of whether or not privileges of the members of the House have been violated in the sense that a minister of the Crown has used his position to move outside of policy guidelines mandated by members of the House.
If we think by analogy of a minister of supply and services who deliberately spent money outside of the public tender process or of a minister in charge of the public service who deliberately avoided the competition process required in the law, we would have to conclude that they would certainly not be acting in a manner consistent with policy guidelines as laid down by members of this House.
What we are dealing with in this question is a set of guidelines regarding the spending of public money. It is very similar to a purchasing policy, or a public service policy, in that particular groups which supply labour services to the government for social purposes have to be selected. To be sure that competition is fair, they have to be selected according to a criterion which is public, which is known to all and equal.
The hon. member for St. John's West raises the issue that in this case those guidelines have not been followed. I believe the suspicion that they were not followed is clearly evident to members of the House and to the Chair. I would suggest that by referring the matter to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections there is an opportunity to call witnesses, to examine the situation and to draw a conclusion which might be fair. If the minister's decision is to be upheld, then any suspicion of misconduct should be laid to rest. However, if the opposite is true, then the House will have to deal with it.
I would urge you, Madam Speaker, to give serious consideration to referring this very important matter to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
These decisions, which the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) described in his intervention, obviously belong to the government. Madam Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege, notice of which I gave Your Honour at noon today. It is in a somewhat different vein than the question of privilege we have been discussing since three o'clock. I realize that what I am about to say will give all my colleagues in the House a splendid opportunity to laugh at my expense. I assure you, Madam Speaker, that I shall not complain. Sometimes I think we might try more often to arrange for laughter. It would be a good tonic to help us cope with some of the things we have to experience here.
In any case, yesterday afternoon I gave vent to a concern I have had for a number of months about the blackening of the Manitoba Tyndall stone over certain vents around the chamber. I asked the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) to investigate the matter to see if some sort of air is being pumped into this place which might be doing something to some of the members of this House.
Immediately after I raised that question, one or two hon. members applauded my concern. One or two others suggested that maybe there were no black spots there, maybe they were just shadows. That gave me some concern. I spent most of the day looking at them. The more I looked, the more convinced I was that those black spots are black spots. Even now there are members looking at them and realizing that those black spots are black spots.
I like to be very sure about these things, so last night I stayed a little later than I usually do.
February 24, 1981

subsubtopic: DSS PAY OFFICES
speechtext:
1.	Was a decision made to have all pay offices operated by the Department of Supply and Services, including central and regional pay offices, operated on one computerized pay system and, if so (a) on what date (b) who made the decision and for what reason?
2.	Was a completely new pay system developed and subsequently abandoned in the mid-1970s?
3.	Which system was chosen, the central or regional, when all offices were moved onto one system?
4.	Were studies undertaken to support the decision to move to one system and recommending the decision to move to that system and, if so, who did the studies and are they available?
5.	Are Privy Council staff paid by a system which bypasses the single computerized pay system and, if so, for what reason?
6.	Is the old central pay system still being used to pay Post Office Department employees?

February 24, 1981
Order Paper Questions
7.	What is the average length of time it takes for a pay increase to take effect for a worker in (a) the Post Office Department (b) departments served by the new central pay system, from the time the increase is granted until it appears on the worker's cheque?
8.	What is the average length of time it takes for employees in (a) the Post Office Department (b) departments being served by the new central pay system, to start receiving regular cheques from the time they commence work?
9.	On what date was the new central pay system implemented?

subsubtopic: DSS PAY OFFICES
speechtext:
1. Yes. In July, 1968, Treasury Board secretariat approved a plan put forward by DSS that envisaged a total payroll system which would allow the Comptroller of the Treasury to standardize procedures and methods while affording the maximum flexibility to respond to user demands for a more effective reporting of expenditures and personnel costs. The plan supported the basic concept for the creation of a central processor containing pay account data on all government employees and common computerized central processing combined with the remote issue of pay cheques and activity reports. A reduced number of pay offices, all operated by DSS, was to be linked with the central processor through communication lines. The reasons given for adopting the new concept were: to meet the demands of collective bargaining being introduced to the public service in 1969 along with various provincial medicare plans; to standardize payroll accounting procedures, improve efficiency and reduce costs, and to meet the central government needs for consolidated and timely reports on personnel information.
2.	Yes. The development of a new pay system based upon central computer processing was begun in 1972; and in the spring of 1974 it had reached the stage of trial conversions to test the proposed system. As a result of these trials it became apparent that the centralized concept had severe limitations and would be incapable of administering the approximately 300,000 pay accounts distributed across Canada. Consequently the decision was taken in November, 1974, to terminate further development of the system.
3.	The regional pay system.
4.	Yes. In late 1974 study groups were formed in DSS to examine the potential of the various options for payroll administration. A formal report was submitted in March, 1975.
5.	The Privy Council staff is paid through the regional pay system.
6.	Yes. The central pay system continues to administer Post Office pay accounts except for term and part-time workers who are paid by local regional services offices.
7.	The length of time for processing a pay increase depends very much on the workload current in the pay office where the account is administered. Recent statistics monitoring work in progress indicate very little time difference between the office processing postal pay accounts from the offices servicing all departments. Although separate reports are not maintained on the processing time for pay increases from other actions the statistics for the last two months show that more than one half the requests received in the pay offices were processed within
two weeks, while 85 per cent were completed within a four-week period. The remaining 15 per cent are currently outside the four-week limit due to a backlog situation created by the CR labour disruptions. It is expected that the temporary backlog will be eliminated by March, 1981. These times do not cover processing within the employee's department. This applies to normal pay increases, however revisions negotiated through collective agreements are permitted a 90-day implementation period.
8.	As indicated in the reply to question 7, there are no significant differences in times between the pay office servicing the Post Office from the pay offices giving service to all departments. Priority is given to the processing of pay of newly joined employees and on these requests our objective is to issue the pay cheque to the employing department within two weeks of the request being received at the pay office.
9.	Following the selection of the regional pay system in 1975 to be the standard system for administering the payroll for all public servants, a development plan was originated for the progressive redesign of the system to meet standards of processing to be set in conjunction with Treasury Board. The enhancement process is continuing today; by April, 1981, the payroll of all departments, with the exception of Post Office, will have been transferred to the regional pay system.

subsubtopic: GRAPHIC DESIGN SECRETARIAT
speechtext: The Graphic Design Secretariat was established as a part of Information Canada for the general purpose of improving the over-all effectiveness, efficiency and quality of graphic design and design management in the government. The secretariat ceased to exist in 1976 with the termination of Information Canada. The secretariat's responsibilities associated with the Federal Identity Program (FIP) were transferred to Treasury Board along with some staff. Two design advisers are presently located in Treasury Board, with responsibilities for developing design standards and policies for the FIP, and for advising government organizations on implementation. FIP objectives and policies are set out in chapter 470 of the Administrative Policy Manual, which is available on request from the Administrative Policy Branch, Treasury Board Canada. Chapter 470 makes reference to the former graphic design secretariat in describing the background leading up to the development of the Federal Identity Program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to introduce economic policies that would restore the economy to its full potential and give Canadians confidence in their future.
He said: Madam Speaker, last Saturday several newspapers in Canada carried the results of a recent Gallup poll in which the people sampled were asked the following question:
Do you think the federal government's policies for tackling the country's economic situation give you a feeling that they are or are not handling the situation properly?
Sixty-one per cent of the population said no, the federal Liberal government is not handling the economy properly. Twenty-five per cent said yes.
Are the people right? Is the federal government handling the country's economic situation properly? No, the people are wrong, said the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in a speech in Montreal yesterday. He said that problems in the economy are not his responsibility as Minister of Finance. They are, he said, the responsibility of the private sector. The problem in our economy, according to the Minister of Finance, is that Canadian workers are greedy and lazy. He did not use that language, obviously; he is too good a politician to do that, but he says that the root cause of our inflation is that Canadians want better wages, pensions and benefits but are unwilling or unable to produce more to finance these benefits. What an affront to the Canadian worker, and what a colossal

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies
cop-out by the Minister of Finance, the man who is supposed to be responsible! Does the minister really believe what he is quoted as saying in his Montreal speech? He said, and I quote:
-the nature of productivity is such that the government can only play a supportive role. Ultimately the productivity revival will have to come from the private sector and from individual initiatives.
If he really believes that, he should resign forthwith. To suggest that the government has only a peripheral effect on productivity is to show either incompetence or dishonesty. One would like to think that the integrity or honesty of the government and its ministers need never be questioned, but, regret-ably, we know from sad experience with this government and its ministers that honesty is not a virtue held in high esteem.
For example, how can we accept or believe in the integrity of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance when he said in his budget that there would not be an export tax on natural gas, but in the next breath announced a charge on natural gas sold to United States consumers? Let me say by way of an aside that I was taught, as I am sure everyone in the House was, that telling the truth is not only morally right, but is in your own best interests as well, because lies have a way of coming back to haunt you. That lesson has just recently been learned by the Minister of Finance.
Currently, the government of Alberta is challenging in court the legality of this charge on gas sold to United States consumers. They have argued in court that this charge is unconstitutional. Counsel for the federal government said that the federal government can certainly impose an export tax, that an export tax is constitutional. When the judge asked counsel for the federal government, "How is it that this charge on natural gas sold to United States consumers was described by the Minister of Finance as not an export tax? He said that there would be no export tax", counsel for the federal government was forced to admit that it was the same thing. The government's own lawyer was forced to admit in front of the judge that the Minister of Finance was not telling the truth when he stated in his budget document that there would not be an export tax on natural gas.
The statement of the Minister of Finance yesterday that the main problem in the Canadian economy is lagging productivity caused by the private sector is exactly in the same category as the statement that there is no gas export tax; it is simply untrue. The main problem with the Canadian economy is the one flagged by Canadian people in the latest Gallup poll, namely, the government's mishandling of the economy. The sad fact is that, in spite of being back in office for a full year now, the government and the Minister of Finance have yet to develop or articulate a coherent economic policy, or any policy, for the matter.
Hugh Anderson wrote an article about the governor of the Bank of Canada which appeared in yesterday's edition of The Globe and Mail. He started the article with a statement which I thought was revealing:
For a man widely credited with running the only national economic policy Canada has, Bank of Canada Governor Gerald Bouey remains remarkably unruffled-
As Mr. Anderson indicated, the only national economic policy of the country at the moment is the tight money policy of the Bank of Canada. Is Mr. Anderson fair in his assessment? Let us look at the record.
Aside from the monetary policy of the Bank of Canada or its responsibility in that area, the government's economic policy comes from the main economic ministers: the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), the Minister of State for Economic Development, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). If a single one of these ministers, or any of the ministers of state associated with them, has yet produced anything which can be recognized as a coherent policy, certainly it has escaped my notice and the notice of almost everyone in the country. Indeed, frequently their actions are at variance with generally-stated goals.
I should like to speak now for a moment about the Minister of Transport.
He has been in office for a full year. The only action he took, or attempted to take, was to try to undo the positive actions of his predecessor, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), regarding the Prince Rupert grain handling facilities. Since then he has done absolutely nothing to improve transportation in this country. In nine months, the hon. member for Vegreville accomplished more than this minister did in a year or more than any of his Liberal predecessors did in their tenures.
Let us consider the Minister of Agriculture. I am not an expert in agriculture, but all I have heard from the Minister of Agriculture in the last year is his repeated statements that he is the world's best minister of agriculture. That is all I have heard, that is all anyone has heard. If there has been an initiative regarding agriculture, certainly it escaped my notice.
Where is the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, that great paragon of virtue, that great human dynamo who was going to change single-handedly the economy of Canada? He was going to repatriate the economy, increase Canadian ownership and lower interest rates. He was going to resign if he could not lower interest rates; he was going to have an industrial strategy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Amazing Gray.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Yes, amazing Gray. Where is the industrial strategy? He was asked about it the other day and he said, "We have to wait for the Constitution". What is the connection between an industrial strategy and the Constitution? This was not explained by the minister. Apparently he and his entire department are twiddling their thumbs, worrying about the Constitution. When they have finished worrying about that, they will get around to developing an industrial strategy.
February 24, 1981

Then there is the minister in the other place, the senator from Alberta, the Hon. Bud Olson, the Minister of State for Economic Development. Has anyone told him what his responsibilities are? Has the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) taken him aside and told him what he is supposed to do? I have been trying to keep track of that minister. I have read the speeches he made across the country in an attempt to discern the responsibilities of that department. They baffle me. I have yet to see any tangible evidence in support of what that minister is doing. He gives speeches and says that they are trying to make an adjustment. "Adjustment" was a key word in his speech to the Quebec Chamber of Commerce. He said:
-we decided early on that we needed some way to ensure that specific federal policies worked together to achieve the right goals. What we came up with was a framework of eight components, the "guts" of the economic development process, if you will.
Then he went on to talk about the eight components. He said:
The eight components are:
-human resources;
-capital investment;
-energy;
-natural resources;
-technology;
-infrastructure;
-market development; and -institutions.
It is a marvellous list. Now let me take a look at what the government has actually produced in terms of the eight components, the guts of the Canadian economic development process which the minister is supposedly overseeing.
Human resources-so far all I have heard is that the government intends to cut the funding to universities by $1,600 million. Will it help promote human resources to cut the guts out of the funding to universities?
Capital investment-I wonder whether the minister can explain how this tight money-high interest policy is helping capital investment. The predictions of the Conference Board of Canada, the Economic Council of Canada, Data Resources of Canada and the Minister of Finance show capital investment going down next year. Where is the substance to back up this goal?
Energy-it has to be a laugh! The energy policy of the government ensures absolutely that we will be short of energy and will be held hostage to the whims of OPEC nations.
Natural resources-has there been a statement, a policy or an announcement on natural resources? If so, it has escaped my notice.
Technology-the government has cut back on its commitment of funds to the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council. The Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) indicated that he expected the private sector to make up the shortfall in the government's spending on research and development. He said the government cannot be counted on to do that.
Economic Policies
Infrastructure, market development and institutions-these are fine words but they have no substance whatsoever.
What about the matter of energy? Government economic ministers, be it the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Finance or the Minister of State for Economic Development use the following phrase, in virtually every speech: "The key to Canada's future is development of our energy potential."
The budget cum energy policy given by the minister last October 28 stated three goals which sound marvellous. No one disagrees with those goals. They are self-sufficiency by 1990, 50 per cent Canadian ownership by 1990, and a fair and equitable revenue-sharing scheme. How could anyone disagree with that? But let us look at what, in fact, has been the impact of this budget cum energy policy. It has been predicted that by the middle of May, half the number of drilling rigs in this country-rigs and equipment which are necessary to explore for the oil and gas which we will need if we are to be self-sufficient-will have left or will be in the process of leaving. That industry is 90 per cent Canadian-owned. It is owned by Canadian citizens living in Canada. This policy, under the guise of Canadianization and self-sufficiency, is driving out half the number of drilling rigs. They are being driven to the United States. And all of this is under the guise of Canadian ownership.
The amount of money which is leaving Canada for greener pastures in the U.S. and offshore as a result of this energy policy is in the billions of dollars-not millions, tens of millions or hundreds of millions, but billions of dollars. This year alone, the estimates are as high as $3 billion, which could and should be invested here in Canada. It is going to the United States. It is not foreign money, Mr. Speaker, but Canadian money. It is money controlled by the Canadian independent oil and gas sector which has been responsible for, on average, 70 per cent of the exploratory wells drilled in Canada over the last ten years. It is the Canadian sector which is designed to Canadian-ize the industry, as stated by the government. That is absolutely absurd.
I would like to deal next with the question of fairness in sharing. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Finance and those who speak in defence of this government's energy policy talk about the necessity of having a fair distribution of the economic rent from oil and gas. The figures they are prone to use for the existing sharing scheme are 45 per cent which goes to the province, 45 per cent which goes to the industry, and only 10 per cent which goes to the federal government. That is simply not true. The fact that they keep repeating this untruth is one of the root causes of the failure of this government to be able to reach an agreement with the provinces. Who would want to negotiate with someone who continues to tell untruths of this kind? Who would want to negotiate with someone who will not accept the facts?
What the government has done, and I use the favourite economic phrase these days of "economic rent", is to establish

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies
the economic rent on a barrel of oil as being S40. By government fiat it has said that it will take approximately 22 of those dollars, which is a little more than half of the $40, and distribute it to the consumers. The government then says it wants to consider sharing the remainder, but it does not want to be asked to consider what has already been distributed by government fiat. To withdraw the $22 from the equation is a form of dishonesty, Mr. Speaker, if not something stronger. Even when the government looks at what is left, the numbers remain cockeyed and concocted to a point which makes them, in fact, untrue. A more realistic comparison has the federal government receiving in the vicinity of 20 per cent, not 10 per cent as it did under the old regime. Certainly, under the new regime it will be a lot more. I do not understand why the government cannot learn that simple lesson. If you want to reach an agreement with someone, the first thing you must do is be honest in your approach. No one will deal with someone they do not trust, not without their hand on their wallet.
If that sounds unduly harsh or critical, Mr. Speaker, I remind the House and the country of a quote which appeared in a newspaper article a few months ago. I believe it appeared in The Globe and Mail and it was about the national energy policy. I believe it was some time in November. In this quote, the assistant deputy minister of energy, one Edmond Clark, who is attributed by many to be the author of the national energy policy, said there was no question that if this were a unitary state we would be paying closer to world price. In other words, the price which is established in this country has nothing to do with the national good. This government does not see itself as having a national mandate; it sees itself as an institution, the federal government, in competition with other institutions in our economy. Therefore, in that competition, since it will be dealing the high cards, the trump, if you will, it will deal harshly so as to ensure that its will prevails. As I said, one of the ways in which this will be done will be by distributing 50 per cent of the economic rent and by talking about sharing the remaining 50 per cent.
I wonder if hon. members opposite ever stop to think about western alienation and the rise in separatism. I wonder if they realize to what extent this may be attributed to the attitude of our national government which says, "Look, we must be interested in the responsibility of the government before that of the country." It may come as a surprise to the Minister of Finance and hon. members opposite that Alberta is a part of Canada. We are a part of the whole. So is Saskatchewan and so is British Columbia. People in Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Alberta are baffled by this thinking. They wonder why the federal government thinks it is virtuous to buy from Mexico at world price but a sin to buy from Saskatchewan, British Columbia or Alberta at three-quarters of the world price. Quite frankly, they do not understand that. I do not think this could be rationalized by a government which thought of Canada and not just of Ottawa.
Then there is that absurd Canadianization program which is nothing more than a nationalization program. There is also the PetroCan tax, which caused a constituent of mine to write a
letter to me which I thought was rather interesting. If you accept the wisdom of the PetroCan tax, wherein the consumers across the country are being asked to pay for the purchase of Petrofina, then why does the government not put the public to a real test and have that PetroCan tax applied only at PetroCan stations? Since this is such a marvellous idea, a constituent of mine wrote to me and suggested that if the government believes in the National Energy Program, then it should establish a national automobile program. His suggestion should appeal to the government. The goals of the national automobile program would be threefold. They would be to establish at least 50 per cent Canadian control of the automobile manufacturing industry by 1990; to assure Canadians of an adequate supply of new cars; and to apply a blended pricing policy which would shelter Canadians from world pricing pressures but which would still allow the federal and provincial governments to receive their fair share of the revenue. I think that would be a marvellous program. My constituent goes on in some detail, but the part that I thought would be particularly appealing to the government is his concept of a federal government Canadianization tax, an "AutoCan tax", if you will, of $500 on each new car sold. A new Crown corporation would be created. This money would be given to Auto Canada, a new Crown corporation. It would use the proceeds of this tax to buy out one of the multinational automobile companies, thereby establishing a 50 per cent ownership of the Canadian automobile business. I think that is great. I think we could next do the same for the clothing business, the mining business, and the pulp and paper business. I mean, it is a winner. All you do is put on this little tax and give the money to a Crown corporation, which can then buy up the foreign-owned industry. It is just a Jim-dandy idea. If the government likes the National Energy Program, they should love this national automobile program and any others which follow.
The National Energy Program is a disaster. I am convinced that it is so bad that the government will have to swallow it within a few months. The question is, how long will it be before they do change their mind? Will the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources realize he has made a mistake sooner, rather than later, to save the country damage from what he is doing? Will the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have the courage to remove him and put somebody else in if the Minister of Energy does not change his mind? Those are the relevant questions.
I suspect that we will go through a few more months of hardship before that happens, but I would be willing to make a considerable wager that this National Energy Program will be altered, because it is absolutely unacceptable. Except for what Mr. Keith Spicer described in a newspaper the other day as "the handful of ideologues" in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, there is not a single person in Canada who supports this program. I do not have enough time to list all the industrial associations which criticize that program- manufacturers, pulp and paper companies, public real estate
February 24, 1981

companies, virtually every industrial organization in the country.
What has the minister of Finance, who has been in office a full year, done in that time other than bring in, over his signature, the National Energy Program? What else has he done? He describes his program to the press as a program of "gradualism". He says he believes in gradualism, and he is gradually trying to make things better, too. What he has, in fact, done is to take a bad situation and make it worse. That is not my opinion; that is the opinion of the experts who make their living assessing the economy and the impact of government action.
The minister introduced a budget which declared war on one industry in one part of the country. That might perhaps be forgivable if there were some over-all benefit to the country, of which there is none, according to the experts.
Let us consider, for a moment, some of the observations being made about the performance of this Minister of Finance as the result of the budget brought in last fall. I have the assessment made by the Conference Board, which is considered to be the expert in short-term projections on the economy. It projected in 1981, just prior to the budget, that gross national expenditures would increase by 1.9 per cent; after the budget, the board dropped its growth projection to 1 per cent. Prior to the budget, the board thought that real disposable income would rise by 2.8 per cent; after the budget its projection dropped to 1 per cent. Before the budget, the board estimated that the consumer price index would rise by 10.5 per cent during the next year; after the budget it said it would be 11.7 per cent.
Instead of having a disastrous situation, we will have a calamitous situation. Productivity, before the budget, was predicted to grow by .8 per cent, which is not much; but after the budget, it was projected to drop by .2 per cent.
The Minister of Finance had the gall to go to Montreal yesterday and say that it is the private sector that is lousing up productivity in our country, and they must pull themselves up by their bootstraps. The Conference Board says that it was the minister's budget which caused a drop of 1 per cent in Canadian productivity. Instead of going up by .8 per cent by next year, as would have been the case before his budget, it will drop by .2 per cent.
The minister says that there is nothing the government can do, and it is up to the private sector. The evidence is right here. It is what the government did and is doing that is driving down the productivity.
What does Data Resources of Canada say? The minister thinks highly of this group, because he quoted them in his budget. They said:
The budget therefore represents one more force weakening the prospective recovery in 1981 to 1982.
This is the independent organization of people who make their living predicting trends in the economy. They say that this budget will make matters worse.
Economic Policies
What does the Economic Council of Canada say? The general impact of the federal budget appears to increase the rate of unemployment. That is what the budget did. The Minister of Finance stood up here during question period today and said that he feels for the people; yet he authored a budget which the Economic Council of Canada says will increase rates of unemployment. He went to Montreal and said, "It is not my fault; it is the private sector's fault; it is the individual's fault. You must pull up your bootstraps and be more productive."
If that is what he feels, why does he not get off people's backs? If that is what he feels, he should stop bringing in stupid budgets like this. If he is concerned about the people of this country, when is he going to put together a coherent set of economic policies? When will he stop relying totally on the governor of the Bank of Canada to implement the one national economic policy we now have, namely a tight money and high interest policy? When will he start balancing that out?
The minister is engaged in what is described as "the big lie technique", the technique of pulling out hair, the gall to state these objectives by using flowery language to describe these attractive goals of Canadianization, increased productivity, more industrial development, and fairer revenue sharing, and then taking action which is exactly opposite to those goals.
When I read the speech which the minister made in Montreal yesterday, I found it difficult to know whether to laugh or cry. Given the total lack of any economic development policies during the past year since this government took over, I wonder whether it is not fair for the Canadian people to ask us to turf these members out of office.
Therefore, I take pleasure in moving this motion, and request that the House give serious consideration to condemning the government for its failure to introduce economic policies which would restore the economy to its full potential and would give Canadians confidence in their future.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these days, a number of words have become almost household terms, such as "unilateral", "divisiveness", "alienation", "separation", and so on; but Canadians around the country have indicated unanimously, whether it be in the halls of the House of Commons, the streets of Ottawa, or in the towns and hamlets in rural areas across Canada, that they have a question, which is, "What, in God's name, is going on there in Ottawa?"
A few days ago, one of the members of the Liberal Party across they way, while discussing the Constitution, indicated that now is the time to patriate our Constitution because it is the last vestige of colonialism in Canada. At the time I did not know whether I should laugh or cry on hearing that comment. Obviously, the individual did not understand the true meaning of colonialism, or he equates it with political symbolism along with economic realities. But if one were to look at the definition of "colony", one would find it is land or territory where resources are exploited for the benefit of a foreign country.

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies
That is us, Mr. Speaker; we are a branch plant country, a colony. For example, let us consider our negative trade balance for fully manufactured goods. In the 1970s, it was nearly $90 billion but in 1979, it was $17 billion for the year, and 1980 was no better.
Just the other day I read in a newspaper that Canada is a rich, developing country and that like all underdeveloped countries, we are experiencing a chronic state of underdevelopment and a chronic state of underemployment.
Let us consider as well the current crisis in the automobile industry, and the past, present and proposed lay-offs in that sector. Let us consider too, the problems being faced by Massey-Ferguson and the deteriorating situation at McDonnell Douglas that was brought to our attention today. There is no question that Canada is being held back by a government which continues to support a branch plant economy; it has indicated clearly time and time again that it has set its mind on a branch plant approach to solving our economic problems.
A "visionary paralysis" would be a good way to describe the government's position and policies. Unfortunately, it is preoccupied with the present and, as the previous speaker indicated, it is preoccupied with the Constitution. It is composed of short-term, tunnel-vision thinkers who spend all their time devising simplistic methods of levying new taxes in an equally simplistic effort to reduce our increasing deficit.
What we need is for some clear national objectives to be established, some clear, definitive intertrade policies, some new long-term Financial policies. If one were to ask members of the government, leaders of business and leaders of labour what the objectives and goals of this government are for 1990, what would the answer be. I suggest that if one looked at the fields of agriculture, mining, forestry, fisheries or self-sufficiency in food production, one would not find the goals clearly stated or precisely identified, either for the government or for Canada.
I must give the government credit for one goal, and that is the goal of ensuring that a measly 50 per cent of the oil industry in Canada is owned by Canadians by 1990. This is a tiny step in the right direction.
We have to ask what the Tories' goals and objectives are. It is easy to recognize that the philosophy of the Liberal Party, by definition, has no long-term goals. What are the goals of the Tories? What are the clearly stated objectives of the Tory party in Canada?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Back to the eighteenth century.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Back to the time of the wealth of nations, of Adam Smith. Presumably they are based on the policies of 1776; the gospel according to the Tories. God help us all.
What Canada needs is for the government to state very clearly now what its job-creation objectives are; what percentage of unemployment should be dropped-should it be 2 per cent or 3 per cent? I think it is a shame that we have come to
agree that 8 per cent or 9 per cent is acceptable. What is our target? What are we aiming for?
We should consider, too, our target in home construction. We say that we are going to build 240,000 homes in Canada this year but why not build 500,000 in the next two or three years? Why not build more decent homes that Canadians can afford?
What is the balance of payments goal for Canada? What are the small business policies designed for the entrepreneur? And as the previous speaker indicated, what is the industrial strategy for Canada? During question period today we heard vague references to the beginnings of an industrial strategy. We have been waiting for it for years and years. The minister responsible for an industrial strategy indicated that he will be saying something about this in the months ahead. He has to spend a considerable amount of time discussing it with the various vested interests concerned, and I am not convinced that it will be to the benefit of Canadians if it is based on the past record of the Liberal Party.
Productivity is a topic that has been before the House a number of times, and it was raised again today by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). He spoke of productivity goals but he had the courage to suggest that the output per worker has decreased and that, by and large, that is one of the crucial factors which hinders Canadian development today, and he said that Canadian workers will have to bite the bullet.
I think it is clear to anyone with even a rudimentary understanding of economics that technology and equipment are problem areas which affect productivity. Money must be spent on research and development, but with a branch plant economy in no way can we expect serious research and development to occur in this country.
Mr. Minister, you have the courage to suggest that Canadian workers are a part of the problem of Canada's lack of productivity and, Mr. Minister, I suspect that we should identify the real problem in this. Indeed, one could suggest it is yourself.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Order, please. I would ask the hon. member to address his remarks to the Chair.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Unquestionably, what this country needs now is strong political leadership to bring government, labour and business together and to address what my leader so aptly identified a number of weeks ago as the pending economic crisis that this country is about to face. We need to establish an open dialogue between these three parties in an effort to create a greater awareness amongst Canadians about our economic problems and to develop positive, co-operative solutions to them.
We have inherited a legacy which is the result of both Liberal and Conservative policies. It emphasizes the competitive and destructive forces in Canada. The problems with our Constitution today are simply a reflection of these difficulties. I refer to the balkanization that has occurred in the regions of Canada and the provinces of Canada. The provinces recognize
February 24. 1981

that they are on their own, that their backs are to the wall, and they can no longer count on the comprehensive co-operative and economic programs of this government because they are simply not there.
Put in simplistic terms, the programs of the Liberals and the Tories have resulted in a directionless, accelerated, goalless exploitation of our resource wealth-dig the coal, dig the copper, export it as quickly as possible, as we did in the days of the fur trade and the squared timber trade during our early economic development.
Although I suspect the Liberals would deny it, they have taken us to the brink of a policy of continentalism over the years which recognizes the North American continent as an economic unit but has not paid much attention to the existence of the 49th parallel.
A few months ago when the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) led the previous government, he gave us another example of a blatant, unbridled rush to an even more aggressive and destructive form of continentalism. Under his policies, Canada would have been even more subservient to the dictates of the North American marketplace.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Joey Reagan.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
The Tories had little to say about a sound Canadian economic strategy. They wanted to return to the time of Adam Smith and the simplistic economies of the eighteenth century. Had the Tories been permitted to continue with their policy, I suspect we would now be in a permanent state of underdevelopment in this country, increasingly dependent on resource exploitation, and increasingly dependent on foreign imports. But Canadians soundly rejected that Tory program.
I hope and pray that the next time around, the people of Canada will soundly reject the hollow and shallow promises being made by the Liberal Party. I do not think there is a better example of a hollow promise than the discussion on research and development that is occurring in Canada today.
Research and development in Canada, except for Ireland and Iceland, places us at the very bottom of the industrialized western nations. At the moment our contribution to R and D is 0.9 per cent, and the minister has the audacity to stand up and say "we hope in five years to have it at 1.5 per cent of our GNP". I suggest that is a Neanderthal approach to research and development. Simply 1.5 per cent will condemn us to falling further behind in the race of western nations to participate in the development of a sound and sophisticated economy. Research and development will not even reach that in five years, as the minister has, in a sense, indicated.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Like a piano player in a cathouse.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
The best measure in research and development is not the percentage of money spent per GNP, but the number of people involved as a percentage of the total population.
Economic Policies
After all, it is not the money poured in for research and development but it is the creative, energetic, innovative minds of people following a clearly defined policy which results in the positive contributory research and development of a country.
Let us look at some figures for a moment. I shall refer now to industrial research and development. The figures I have selected are from 1977. The situation, of course, has not changed since then, some have even suggested that it has worsened.
In 1977, Canada, with a population of 23 million, employed 22,000 people in industrial research and development, whereas Sweden, with 8 million people, employed 24,000 people; Holland with 14 million people had 26,000 employed; France, with 54 million people, had 120,000 employed; West Germany, with 61 million people, had 197,000 people employed; Japan, with 115 million, had 306,000 employed; and the United States of America, with 217 million, had 394,000 people involved in industrial research and development.
All of these countries, with the exception of Canada, have on stream at the moment aggressive five-year plans to double and triple those numbers of individuals involved in research and development. What is so shameful is that Canada has no goal in this area in any meaningful way. Why is this? We have to ask why it is that we are so far behind and seemingly falling further and further behind. Either a great difference exists between our industrial objectives, policy or strategy and those of other countries, or we simply do not know what is going on. I am sorry to say that I am forced to accept the latter, that we do not seem to know where we are going. We do not seem to know what our economic objectives are in this country. Consequently, we are unable to have a decent post-secondary educational policy or a research and development policy because we do not know what it is we are trying to accomplish. As the previous speaker indicated, the government is suggesting consideration of cutbacks of $1.5 billion in post-secondary educational funding. This is at a time when more money should be spent in those areas in an effort to invest in the future of Canada than is being spent now.
In conclusion, we could end up in the next few weeks with a Constitution that is the envy of the world. However, if we are not careful, we will end up with a situation in Canada without the economic wherewithal to really do anything with the Constitution.

Is this another budget?

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
I must say I am not obliged to thank him for giving me any ideas as to how to manage the economy. In fact, the resolution which he has moved condemns the government for its failure to produce economic policies which would allow the economy to reach its full potential. In the course of his speech, the hon. member made not a single constructive suggestion which could be described as economic policy. In fact, the Conservative Party is groping, day after day, for a policy of some kind and it does its groping before us all during the question period as it searches for an economic policy. Because there is no co-ordination and because there is no real thought given to the question of the economy, contradictory statements are made day after day. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), supported by his seatmate, the former president of the treasury board, led an attack on what they consider to be government extravagance, the failure of the government to be more restrained, the failure of the government to reduce the deficit and the failure of the government to reduce even further the rate of spending.
That is that wing of the party. The other wing, for example, is represented by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), who, day after day, asks for more spending and more social programs. At times, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) joins that group when he calls for energy tax credits, and so on. I intend to say more about that later and I intend to say a bit more about the usually contradictory and often dangerous medicines prescribed by the official opposition for the Canadian economy.
First, I want to describe to the House some recent developments in the Canadian economy which are not only welcome but, in my view, are further evidence that the balanced, non-extremist approach, adopted in the October budget was the wisest course of action to take in the present situation in Canada. I stated in that budget that I rejected extreme solutions on either side. I stated quite clearly that I wanted to follow a moderate course and avoid the dangers of the extremists' positions, one adopted by the New Democratic Party and the other, not adopted by the Conservative Party but by the hon. member for St. John's West when, in his more right-wing moments, his true colours come to the surface, and he is permitted by the red Tories to show that bit of blue which designates his colours.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: The Liberal Party is the party of the dead centre.
