subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: The most recent information I have on the economy, Mr. Speaker, makes it clear that there was an unexpectedly strong recovery in the economy in the second half of 1980.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: We all missed it. Where was it?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: The growth in real output during the third quarter was at an annual rate of 1.7 per cent. The fourth quarter figures will become available at the end of this week, and I expect they will show a growth rate of more than 6 per cent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
I think that is rather remarkable in light of the gloom and doom which has been voiced by members of the opposition.
Therefore, for the year 1980 as a whole we may see a small increase in growth rather than a decrease in real growth which we expected at budget time. That recovery and that strength in the economy is most welcome and will be appreciated, I am sure, by all members of the House.
Another development is that employment has continued to rise. Almost one quarter of a million new jobs were created last year. Unemployment is still high but it is less than 7.5 per cent, less than I expected in the October budget. Of course, the main reason for this recent strength in the economy is the remarkable strength of our foreign trade. Our trade surplus in the fourth quarter was more than SI 1 billion. This is a record figure and probably exceeded our deficit on non-merchandise transactions. We may have had the first current account surplus since the first quarter of 1974. That is what is happening to the economy.
As well, there has been some recovery in consumer spending and housing helped by the decline in interest rates last summer and fall.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: What decline in interest rates?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
That decline may have gone unnoticed by the hon. member for Calgary Centre. In light of his comments this afternoon, I would say he has not noticed a lot of things that have happened in this country and in this Parliament. I do not want to exaggerate, but there has been some recovery in consumer spending and housing, helped, as I said, by the decline in interest rates last summer and fall as well as by the increase in employment.
To do this well in the troubled world environment we are now facing is evidence of the fundamental strength of Canada's economy. We could not achieve those trade figures without a strong competitive power. Our competitive power is strong because our costs have risen less than in most industrial countries and because our exchange rate is favourable to our exporting countries.
It is obvious that other countries envy our rich resources. The products of our mines and forests have swelled our export figures. As one of the world's great exporters of grain, we are benefiting from high international prices. These are some of the positives that one ought to lay on the record in discussing the Canadian economy. Of course, our varied sources of energy are of immense value. One of our greatest challenges is to ensure that we develop them in ways which will serve the interests of all Canadians.
I noted the comments made by the hon. member for Calgary Centre on the National Energy Program. It is obvious that he holds these views very strongly. They are not my views, not the views of the government or of the Liberal Party. Our views are quite different from those held by the hon. member for Cal-
February 24, 1981

gary Centre. The sooner we recognize that there is a vast difference between this party and the party opposite, the better understanding we can reach in the debates in this House of Commons.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Tell us what is the difference.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is seeing one of those black spots. He is the one who told us that Members of Parliament sometimes see things that are not there. He has been having one of his attacks in the last moment or two.
We have also secured impressive success in the new growth areas of high technology. I am delighted that my speech in Montreal received as much attention as it did today. I have unusual experiences in my life. 1 am accused by the hon. member for St. John's West of being silent. When I break my silence, the first man to complain is the hon. member for St. John's West. However, I broke it yesterday and talked about the impressive success that the Canadian economy has had in the area of high technology.
In my speech I talked about the Dash-8, the Challenger, the PT-6 and Telidon. All of these are world class examples of Canadian technology. We need to develop more. The emphasis which the spokesman for the NDP, the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) placed on research and technology is a priority which I share and which this government shares. That is why we have placed in our spending plans a high priority on the general area of economic development. One of the most important components in that area is further support for research and development, a well-placed emphasis which was echoed by the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap.
I would like to say as well that the regional patterns of economic growth are changing in Canada. I did not hear very much from the opposition this afternoon about the regional character of the Canadian economy, how varied the economy is and how different the rates of growth are in various parts of the country. We all know of the dramatic growth in the western provinces.
Let me tell the hon. member for Calgary Centre that my Canadianism is not restricted to my own region. I am delighted that Alberta is currently showing a strong rate of growth and Saskatchewan has a healthy rate of growth. British Columbia has a problem with housing and services. Why? Because of strong economic activity.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: You will notice there are no Liberals there. Do you think it is a coincidence?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
I want to emphasize that the pattern of growth is different in various regions. There is a strong and promising growth in western Canada. I assure the hon. member for Calgary Centre that the National Energy Program will assist and facilitate the further development and growth of western Canada rather than impede that growth, as he suggested in his speech. I will be ready to stand by that
Economic Policies
prediction a year or two down the road when the economy will be strong and definite.
There is a new promise of growth in Atlantic Canada. There is no longer any doubt that we have a major commercially viable oil field in Hibernia. There are new markets for the coal of Nova Scotia and new potential for the fisheries of Atlantic Canada as a result of the development of the 200-mile limit.
Let us not put down this country in an economic debate. Let us look at some of its strengths and acknowledge its weaknesses as well. There are weak spots in the Canadian economy. The weakest spots recently have been in the automobile industry, in the farm implements industry and in some other manufacturing industries located mainly in Ontario.
We have taken steps to support the automobile industry in this particularly difficult adjustment period. We have taken steps to assist the farm implement industry. We are absolutely determined to ensure that the manufacturing industry achieves its potential for further growth and development. I did not find the same pessimism among the businessmen who spoke to me before my budget, especially from the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. Their message to me was that we have regained our competitive position; we had lost it, but we have regained that position; we are in a good position now to compete vigorously and aggressively internationally; and "Please don't do anything in your budget through additional corporate taxes that will impede our future growth and development."

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
The main problems we face in Canada are closely interlinked. The first is the slowdown in productivity, and the second is the accelerating rate of inflation. These are the two problems we face as an economy. I have heard not a word from spokesmen opposite as to how we should cope with these seemingly intractable problems. One gets the impression that they are intractable as one sees each industrialized country wrestle with declining productivity. Even Germany and Japan, the model economies of the world, are struggling with the problem of declining productivity.
So what do we do about it? 1 receive no answers from members of the opposition. These are worldwide problems, but that does not make them any less serious for Canada. In my address yesterday I pointed out that output per worker has actually declined since 1973 after rising by nearly 3 per cent per year in the previous 12 years. That has happened in our economy; there is no point in attempting to avoid staring it in the face.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
How come it happened?

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
It has happened for a variety of reasons, but it is important to understand that when one uses output per worker as a measure of productivity, that is not casting any slur on the workers of this country. When we use that expression, it is used as a measure. It is not an evaluation of how hard individuals work. It is not a moral judgment nor a political judgment; it is simply a way of measuring the productivity of our country.
What I was saying yesterday in Montreal is that if we in this country want-as I think we should have in the future-better standards of living, better security for the needy, better pensions and better wages, the only way we can reach that is through increasing productivity. There is no other way.
I made the statement that as a nation we are entitled only to what we produce. We are entitled to the gross national product, to nothing more and to nothing less. Rising entitlements can only be legitimized through increased economic growth. I demonstrated that because during the period 1961 to 1973 the gross national product nearly doubled. But how did that come about? It came about because of rising productivity. In the last seven years, since 1973, there has been declining productivity. Even though the rate of growth in employment has been about the same, we are now facing a situation in which we have the phenomenon of declining real incomes. If we want to turn that around, we have to do a number of things, and I discussed these matters quite fully in the address I gave yesterday.
Of course, inflation is a very serious problem. Prices have been rising rapidly ever since the early 1970s. There was some relief in 1976 and 1977 as a result of the anti-inflation program. Food prices declined at that time, but they have been accelerating steadily since then. The cost of living rose more than 10 per cent last year, and in January of this year, it was 12 per cent higher than a year earlier. We have not done quite as badly as some other countries, but we have not done as well in meeting the challenge of inflation as have Germany and Japan, which have done better than Canada. However, we have done better than quite a number of other countries.

speechtext: Name one.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
We know that inflation is bad, unjust and discriminatory. It has strong elements of injustice because it affects different groups in the economy and in society differently. Retired pensioners, for example, and those who are not strong in the economy suffer most. That is why inflation is bad from a social point of view, but it is also bad from an economic point of view because it prevents us from reaching our full potential in the way of economic growth and in the way of employment growth.
The fact is that at the present time inflation is deeply embedded in our system. It is embedded not only in the system but also in the psychology of the population, all of us. That psychology has to be turned around. It will not be turned around quickly.
There are those who believe it can be turned around very quickly by what I consider to be punitive economic policy measures, by turning the screws and by pursuing policies
which will have an effect on inflation and probably bring the rate of inflation down more rapidly through deep expenditure cuts, for example, or strong doses of monetary policy. Those things may bring down the rate of inflation, but at what expense? At the expense of declining output and rising unemployment.
If hon. members say to me, "Why don't you bring down inflation more rapidly through this type of measure," my answer is simply that I feel that the social costs are too great and that there is more to economic policy than the policy itself. One has to examine its impact on the community and society, what it will do and how well it will be supported by the population. All the evidence is not in on this particular question, but I would not recommend to my colleagues nor to Parliament a policy which would be Draconian in its application through monetary and fiscal policy in order to reduce inflation rapidly.
That is why I have opted for a policy of gradualism. I believe over time that would produce the results with the least possible damage to the economy and society. That is the stance I adopted in the budget, and it is still my stance.
All that has happened since the budget reinforces the necessity for a strong anti-inflationary stance in the economy. Let me repeat very briefly the elements of that anti-inflationary stance. First of all, there is the necessity for restrained growth in the money supply. The Bank of Canada has been successful in meeting its progressively lower growth targets and has had the government's full support in doing so. The reduction in the target band from 5 per cent to 9 per cent to 4 per cent to 8 per cent, recently announced by the governor of the bank, is a further step in this steady approach to achieving the monetary conditions for non-inflationary growth.
I fully support the further step of the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Of course our job and the job of the Governor of the Bank of Canada in administering monetary policy in Canada has been made more difficult by the volatility of the interest rates in the United States which we have all observed. Faced with these conditions, in my opinion the Bank of Canada has struck a reasonable balance between moderating the impact on Canadian interest rates and on the exchange rate.
When American interest rates rise and remain higher than Canadian ones, as they did for a good part of 1980 and the beginning of 1981, there is a pressure on Canadian interest rates and the exchange rate. You take it on either or on both. The governor has struck what I thought was a balanced approach by taking it on both. It is a matter of judgment. I do not think anyone has found a better way.
The fiscal policy is another element of our anti-inflationary stance. We are determined to reduce the deficit and our financial requirements. Relative to the size of the economy, our deficit and financial requirements this year have been held below the peak levels reached in 1978-79. Deficits as a percentage of the gross national product are projected to be cut in
February 24, 1981

half over the next three years under the budget's tax and expenditure plan.
So, we are winding down the deficit. But, why not a faster reduction of the deficit? In 1980 there was some weakness in the Canadian economy. If we had reduced the deficit and decreased expenditures more rapidly, we would have increased the weakness of the Canadian economy. That had to be taken into account. We intend to hold government expenditures to or below the trend growth of the gross national product. This is not only important from the point of view of reducing inflation, but also to ensure room, resources and incentives for sustained private sector growth. We will be able to achieve deficit reduction while hopefully avoiding general, personal or corporate income tax increases, further helping the economy to achieve its potential.
Obviously comparisons are drawn between our fiscal stance and the measures proposed by the President of the United States. I have no intention of prescribing for the United States economy; that is the exclusive responsibility of the authorities of the United States. But I would say that in substantial part, for example, the tax measures of the president represent a catching up to a system already in place in Canada. United States personal income tax cuts will not go much further than to make up for the past and prospective increases which result from the lack of indexation in that country. I believe the tax relief for 1981 which will be afforded to the Canadian taxpayer through indexation is greater than the tax relief which will be afforded through the cuts proposed by the president.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Also I would add that the proposed new depreciation rates in the United States leave our industry, especially manufacturing, in quite a favourable position relative to that country.
The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) asked me to take guidance from the economic package of the President of the United States. As I said, it is not for me to prescribe for the United States, but if we undertook at the present time the deep expenditure cuts inherent in the president's proposal, if we, for example, decided to reduce our expenditures to a rate of growth of 6 per cent per year, as is the presidential objective, we could not do so without harming basic fundamental social programs of vital importance to Canadians.
I believe that by 1983-84 the rate of growth in government expenditures will be about 10 per cent. In order to achieve this, we will have to secure a saving of $1.5 billion in intergovernmental transfers. We do not know where those savings will occur yet. The hon. member is premature in saying that they will occur from post-secondary education; that has not been decided. But even to achieve the savings I am projecting, which are less onerous than the ones projected in the United States, it is essential that we secure not only savings within our own programs but savings in intergovernmental transfers.
This is our gradualist stance; over time we will reduce inflationary pressures by following a moderate, gradual, medi-
Economic Policies
um-term, fiscal monetary and expenditure plan. That is where we are at as a Liberal Party. I believe this moderate course will ensure that the Canadian economy in the 1980s will achieve its full potential, that productivity and investment will be improved, and that we will not fall victim to some of the more extreme economic policies advocated from time to time by members of the opposition.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, certainly the presentation of the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) was from a purely political point of view. His arguments had very little relationship to economics or fiscal and monetary policies. He justified everything he has done.
It reminded me of being in the House during my first session when I believe the Hon. John Turner was minister of finance. It has been said on several occasions that that was the turning point in the Canadian economy, the turning point from management to mismanagement in basic government programs which affect the entire economy of the nation.
I remember seeing Mr. Turner standing in approximately the same location as the present Minister of Finance and defending policies which were critized by economists, businessmen, and the rank and file of the people as not being in the best interests of Canada. He defended them with an evangelistic fervour which has been unequalled in the House, even by the present Minister of Finance. It was the beginning of the decline in Canada's economy. Eventually that gentleman saw the folly of the ways of the Liberal government and without a word left the government, and properly so. The only regrettable thing is that he made his contribution to our present economic crisis-and we are very close to a crisis-and left without giving Canada any guideline as to what might better be done for this country than he was able to do following Liberal politicians and their bureaucratic recommendations. Today is a repetition of the bureaucratic recommendations which were obvious in the program of the then minister of finance to whom I have just referred.
This is a divisive program. It cannot be described in any other fashion. The Minister of Finance has stated that it is his objective to save $1,500,000,000 in cost-sharing programs, grants to the provinces, etc. All this is doing for Canada is transferring the tax responsibility and the service responsibility from the federal Minister of Finance and the federal Grits to whomever may be unfortunate enough to find himself in power in any province in Canada.
His dismissal of the idea that secondary education may suffer as a result of the reduction in the distribution of wealth to the provinces is just not worthy of a man of the intelligence which he is supposed to have. There is no question that if $ 1,500,000,000 is pulled back from the provinces, then services rendered by those provinces must suffer or they, in turn, must tax. Can the provincial governments then expect the political

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies
repercussions which emanated from the Minister of National Elealth and Welfare (Miss Begin) when in campaign against provincial governments and, in defence of the federal government she criticized the health programs of virtually every province in Canada after she had tried to cut the purse strings before they left Ottawa? That is the policy which this government is again projecting. It will reduce the grants to the provinces in one way or another. There is no question but that those programs in those provinces will suffer.
One provincial minister of health in Canada has said that there is no way that progressive policies which have been adopted historically can be followed. He says that they may be able to maintain the present medicare program and the present hospital program. He says that they have been trying to supply auxiliary services which have been expanding on a regular basis, but if there is a cut in the federal funds awarded for health to the provinces then that will be the end of the progressive programs of which he has been so proud. We will come to the position where we shall tax the provinces, if there is to be any progression in health. And so it goes throughout the provincial programs which have been so dependent upon the largesse of the Liberal government in Ottawa, which largesse is apparently shrinking today.
I was rather amused when the Minister of Finance said that he spoke to businessmen before handing down his budget. I wonder how many of them have given him the privilege of an address since he handed down his budget. His performance has certainly not pleased the business community. It has not pleased consumers. It has not pleased the manufacturers or the wholesalers' associations, or any other group. I wish I had time to give the minister some quotes to support this. Even that loyal paper, The Toronto Star, had a recent item on February 12 condemning the policies of the government in respect of its application of interest rates and the cost of doing business. The minister does not want a Draconian policy, but he is forcing one upon the provinces of Canada. Indeed, the provinces will take the blame and not the federal government, if there is any way that it can be transferred by the Liberal government to them.
We have conducted ourselves in a fashion which is very comparable to the German fiasco of inflation immediately after World War I. I challenge you who support this government to read the various steps which took place, and to compare the identical cash flow situation in Germany after World War I with the cash flow situation which we have here today. Yes, we have a favourable trade balance. No, we do not have a favourable balance of payments cash flow in this country. What is worse is that we must depend upon foreign sources for our borrowings and unless our exports go up immensely and our imports go down drastically then our cash flow, our balance of payments, will get worse, as it did in Germany after World War I.
The reasons are different. The reason over there was that they had payments to make as reparations to those countries which were victorious in that war. Our reasons are that we are spending in excess of our means. We are sending money out of
this country in the form of interest and in other forms of cash flow, such as loans to other countries at no reasonable interest rate. We are not aware of just what the consequences of the unfavourable balance will be in the towers of Ottawa, as we build it and continue to build it by further deficit financing and further borrowing abroad.
There are those who have said of inflation that it just is possible that once it has reached the double-digit stage it is irreversible and that there is not the will of government. That is what the Minister of Finance said today. He said he does not have the will or the political courage. He said that he does not have the courage to apply to Canada those economic measures which could, in fact, reverse the inflationary tendencies which are so devastating to the total welfare of our economy.
I think you would find that at the moment, Mr. Speaker, we are resorting to any means possible. We are borrowing. We are giving the Canadian people a mild sedative to ease the pain for the short term. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the delusions of the opiate are there ahead of us in the long term, if we do not resort to a responsible position.
Let us take a look at a few of the little things that happened in 1980 versus the things which the minister was talking about today with respect to employment. According to statistics, the rate of job creation under this government is one half of that achieved by the previous government in its short term in office. We can take those months and compare them. But there is something even worse than that. The rate of employment in the private sector is only one quarter today of that of 1980. The real job creation has taken place in the public sector, at public expense-at taxpayers' expense. That is where the job creation has taken place. The minister smiles, but he is fully aware of that.
The rate of employment in the public sector has gone up 12 times in 1981, or since February of 1980 until today. So it is easy, as long as the taxpayers will pay the bill, to have job creation at public expense. But it is more challenging and beyond the scope of the imagination of this government to create an economic atmosphere in which employment will take place in the private sector.
The minister referred today to the psychology of inflation, those things that people anticipate and want. He has not referred to the government policy which might in any way deflate those inflationary expectations. He says he is going to turn the screws, but not on himself, rather on the provinces.
The two problems of productivity and inflation to which he has referred are real. I share his concern about the existence of both. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that as long as interest rates are as high in this country as they are, any small businessman-and small business employs about 60 per cent of all Canadians-is very hard-pressed to see the logic. To obtain a more productive plan, when the interest rate at this moment in time will cost more than the savings in higher productivity, is self-defeating. The only way we will achieve higher productivity is when the incentive for it is there in earnings for the labourer and in earnings for the employer. Both are absolutely
February 24, 1981

essential. There is a feeling of insecurity. No one knows which way the government will move next to collect its money.
I said in this House earlier, in another debate, that I agree with the Minister of Finance that, in fact, we do have an international problem. In fact there are similar policies in other countries. We do have interest rates which are too high-not only in Canada but in other countries. I submit this is self-defeating, if we cannot get together with some of the others who find themselves indubitably in the same position of declining standards of living.
We can talk about rights, we can talk about defence; we can talk about any number of matters on an international basis. Why does this nation not take the initiative and call an international conference to determine how, where and when we can get down to the point where people can afford to live? It is not impossible.
If we are as concerned as we claim to be about the Third World and about Canada-and we can express little interest in the Third World, economically, if we do not express an interest in prosperity at home-why have we as a government not obtained for this nation some opportunities to get rid of some of the products which others need and which we can produce in abundance? We are prepared to sell our raw materials to Japan. We need to sell them; I recognize that, but we have very much been denied the right to sell beef or agricultural products on the Japanese market. This activity is increasing very slowly.
We drive down the street, and we meet Japanese cars, but it will be very difficult to go to Japan and find a Canadian french fry- maybe a few. There are obstacles there which we must remove, and if the Minister of Finance wants that era of prosperity to recover, we must negotiate and develop a twoway street. We have a European Economic Community. Why are we not trying to put fish, agricultural products, building products, and pre-fab houses into their market? Why should we take the various European vehicles-cars, among other things? A Japanese car is not the only item which comes into this country from which we derive no employment benefit for the people of this nation, except when someone is needed to drive it up to meet a customer.
I ask the Minister of Finance, the trade ministers of this country, when did we list last get a contract in the European Economic Community for an up-to-date telephone system, an electronic system? I agree with the Minister of Finance who said that Canada has probably got the best technology in the world. But we are not successful in our tenders on these items which can turn the economy around in this nation, and all this is coupled with an element of desire on the part of the minister to turn the screws on himself instead of on the provinces, which is his present objective.

speechtext: Right on.

speechtext:
The Minister of Finance claimed that there are regional problems. Indeed, there are. There is regional
Economic Policies
difficulty in the industrial structure of Ontario. So we are, and I do not complain about this, offering assistance and incentives to the manufacturing industry, the auto industry and the machinery industry. Good! But what makes me angry is that we talk about Massey-Ferguson, with its 6,000 plus employees in Canada, getting SI00 million, maybe $200,000 million in assistance from the Government of Canada. However, in the Atlantic region, we have 100,000 people in fishing boats, in processing plants, and in boat manufacturing groups, 100,000 people engaged in that industry. And we are not getting as assistance to that fishing boat industry, the equipment to modernize that fleet, and we are not getting the equivalent of the interest on the aid which has been extended to Chrysler and to others in that category. That is the division which exists, and that is why there is regret in Atlantic Canada that there are these problems. There are divisions.
In this country we are trying to apply a single forest policy across Canada, and yet in Atlantic Canada we have the budworm to a degree that no other part of Canada has. We cannot get the co-operation of this government to develop proper sprays, insecticides, pesticides, proper applications to preserve that forestry. One third of all the working people in New Brunswick are employed in forestry. But there is nothing coming forward there, nothing comparable to the assistance that is given to Chrysler.
I do not regret the assistance to Chrysler. I regret the division that the Minister of Finance mentioned. Why does he not exert some influence?
What about agriculture? I mentioned the necessary trade policies that we need, that if we are going to take all the goods from the European Economic Community, the Japanese, et al, then let us get some goods in there as well. Agriculture needs assistance. It needs a port in St. John's and in St. Andrews. It needs trading opportunity. Again, we are not getting the equivalent of the interest on the aid that has been extended to industry in central Canada. There is no quarrel with aiding central Canada, but let us not be divisive or regional, and let the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) speak up for those regions which need the help. They are very obvious by their silence, while people in need suffer.
The minister mentioned Hibernia. What is the story of Hibernia? If you talk to anybody who has any knowledge of that Hibernia oil field, what will they tell you? We are not going to proceed with development in the most productive way until such time as the federal government ends its era of uncertainty, until it gets down to brass tacks and tells us where we are going.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
We talk about uncertainty. The government has given the country misinformation. It has said that it was new information when it was old. There is not any question but that all the statements which were made in this House, for instance about the removal of oil rigs from the west, were right and up to date, but the Minister of Energy, Mines and

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies
Resources quoted figures which were two or three months old, and they were quoted to the public as if they were gospel.
On one day, when those figures were given in this House, I found that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) knew how many rigs were going out, that the oil industry in Alberta knew how many were up on blocks and not working, but the Minister of National Revenue misled this House and the people of Canada to believe that the figure was one half of the 180 which were out of production. That is the uncertainty, the lack of trust which has been generated. No, you do not have to be Draconian, but you must show leadership.
The minister must show leadership in order to get the steel mill going in Sydney, an area that he represents. He must show leadership and courage as Minister of Finance in order to get the offshore resources going and to remove uncertainties and give them the regulation they need. We need the money that these things will produce, and there must be planning if that is to be forthcoming. We cannot go on in this way, with rail line abandonment and the removal of express services in Atlantic Canada. Some of the little communities will shrivel and die because they cannot get services. Only yesterday I received a message from a little village which is 25 miles from the nearest express service. It has been told there will be no more deliveries. And beyond that village there are people who live 50 miles from the CP Express service, and it is to be removed. These things are divisive, Mr. Speaker. They are divisive to western Canada, to Atlantic Canada, and to central Canada.
Let us start to serve Canada, Mr. Speaker, with an economic policy that builds, develops, and creates incentive. Let us not discourage people with high interest rates. Let us get on the track.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the speeches given today by members of the official opposition and the opposition, and especially to the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). I think that his was one of the best speeches and explanations of the government's economic policy ever given in this House. I am sure it was able to illuminate the government's policy clearly and concisely for hon. members opposite and for the public who may have been watching television.
The minister indicated that the government's policy is a balanced approach to gradual reduction of the deficit over time; the maintenance of social programs, of the basic core of the social programs that have been the backbone of this country and which have been a model for the rest of the world; the movement of our priorities within the envelope system toward greater economic development; incentives for energy development, and the National Energy Program. This is a program that I am proud of in spite of the comments of hon. members opposite. The minister has indicated that he is proud
of it. We think it is the right policy and program and that in the years to come it will prove itself as being the right approach.
A great deal of misinformation has been passed around by hon. members opposite and the media about the nature and effects of the National Energy Program. I intend to deal with some of these in my speech, Mr. Speaker.
There has been a great deal of debate in the House in past months, particularly by the official opposition, which indicates that they believe the government does not have priorities, that it should undertake programs in a number of other areas, that spending should be increased, the deficit should be reduced, interest rates lowered, and that inflation should not be stimulated. I think hon. members of the official opposition will admit, if they think clearly about it, that to do all the things we have been advised to do would lead to utter and absolute economic chaos in the country. We cannot do all the things that hon. members opposite recommend. You cannot increase spending at the same time as you reduce spending; you cannot decrease the rate of inflation and at the same time dramatically decrease interest rates. Those things are inconsistent.
I would ask hon. members opposite, I would plead with them, to put the policy proposals they have into some kind of framework so that they can be understood and are consistent. If one thing has become clear with regard to the economic policy and the economic pronouncements of the opposition in past months, it is their total inconsistency. If the opposition expects the government to listen, it will have to take a consistent position on major matters of economic policy such as the deficit, inflation, growth and development. It must tackle the questions of cutting the deficit, of reducing government spending on the one hand and on the other increasing massively the money available for research and development, for industrial adjustment, industrial relocation, retraining programs, energy tax credits, subsidies on home heating oil, and so on. It must resolve how we can meet the problem we have with the province of Alberta about the price of oil, which it would like to see much higher, while at the same time we hold down the price of oil to the consumer.
When I read the motion put forward by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) I almost regarded it as a laughing matter. It has become clear during the past months that the opposition has no idea what a coherent, consistent economic policy is, one that recognizes all the factors to be considered in developing a policy that is in the interests of the entire nation.
We have to be concerned with unemployment at the same time that we are concerned with inflation. We have to be concerned with economic growth and development at the same time we are concerned with reducing the deficit. These things have to be balanced. In October last the Minister of Finance brought forward a budget that took a balanced approach and which will lead to a reduction in the deficit.
As the minister said, we could take a Draconian approach. I do not say, for example, that the United States has taken a Draconian approach, but from the point of view of expenditure
February 24, 1981

cuts their approach is much harder than the approach taken in this country.
I believe, as I think hon. members opposite believe, that our social policies form a sound, solid basis of social security for Canadians. They are a consistent, coherent set of policies and form a sound basis. Perhaps that is not the case in the United States and, as a result, perhaps the President of the United States in his wisdom believes that he could undertake much deeper cuts in some social programs than I believe we could in Canada. To make such cuts in Canada would undermine the basic integrity of our social security system and, to my mind, that is totally unacceptable.
There have been some accusations made against the government in the past, particularly in the debate on borrowing authority. The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) and others regard the budget which he introduced in December of 1979 as a standard against which this government should be measured and against which the last budget should be measured. Today the hon. member for Calgary Centre implied that if the hon. member for St. John's West had been allowed to implement that budget the country would be in better shape, the deficit would have been reduced further and faster, interest rates and inflation would be lower, and there would be greater economic growth and development, the business community would be in better health, and so on. That is incorrect, Mr. Speaker. In a speech I made last week I indicated why it is not correct. Our budget indicates clearly that we are going to show a reduction in the deficit, and that our financial requirements will decline by an amount similar to that which would have been achieved had the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West been implemented.
Yesterday the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) spoke in Cornwall and indicated that when his government was in power a year ago it had a plan to cut the national deficit by $5 billion. He noted that at present our total deficit is $14 billion and indicated that the deficit under the Conservative government would have been much smaller. If all factors are considered, if we are intellectually honest and analytically correct in evaluating the situation, we will find that the deficit was grossly understated in the December, 1979, budget.
First, if we just look at late winter and the early spring of 1980 we find that the dramatic oil price increases were not anticipated in that budget. That alone would have increased the deficit facing the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West by some $2.3 billion this year as a result of the higher oil import compensation payments. Hon. members opposite can say "no, that is not correct, we would have done something about it". But what would they have done? Would they have reduced the oil import compensation payments? Would they have increased oil prices much faster than they promised in the budget? We never hear these kinds of things when hon. members say that they would have done so much better.
The hon. member for St. John's West has admitted the recession would have led to a deficit, and I will quote him
Economic Policies
again, "a few hundred million dollars" higher than he had projected in that budget, and with it interest costs. Over all, the deficit under that December, 1979, budget would have been $2.7 billion to $3 billion higher than the forecast found in the December, 1979, budget. If those figures were put together, hon. members would find that the deficit in the December, 1979, budget and the reduction between now and 1983-1984 would have been no better than the deficit reduction found in the budget of October 28, 1980, presented by the Minister of Finance.
If hon. members look at financial requirements, under the October 28, 1980 budget, they are to be reduced faster, and by a greater amount, than the financial requirements would have reduced under the budget of December, 1979. The facts are there, Mr. Speaker. Hon. members can evaluate the data I have put forward to them and I will be glad to explain it all to them in person if they need more help. I hope this indicates that, given the situation confronting this economy, the budget which the minister has put forward is a responsible, reasonable, and the best possible response to those economic situations.
We also hear that we have a high interest rate policy in Canada. In the past the minister has put forward an explanation of how these excessively high interest rates have come about. It is said honestly and in a straightforward manner that because of the federal reserve policy in the United States, there has been a rapid rise in interest rates there. In turn, that has caused an outflow of capital from Canada, causing our interest rates to follow theirs. If our interest rates did not follow those of the United States, the Canadian dollar would drop even further. The Bank of Canada policy, the policy supported by the minister and by the government, is a balanced response which takes some of the pressure in higher interest rates, some of the pressure in the decline of the dollar, and will try to balance out these pressures.

Hon. members opposite have said in the past and today that that is not true, that the United States policy had nothing to do with Canada or very little to do with Canada, that our policies are being brought about by mismanagement of the government or are being brought about by a government which does not care. Helmut Schmidt in Germany, according to a press report the other day, said that he was greatly disturbed by that very policy in the United States because it was placing extreme pressure on the Deutschmark and other Euro-currencies in the European Common Market. It bears out what the minister put forward in the past, namely, that the U.S. policy has had a dramatic effect. When you consider the proximity of our two countries and the ease with which capital flows between Canada and the United States, the effect on us has been even

Economic Policies
greater than the effect on those countries. When one considers that Canada is comprised of 24 million people versus 240 million in the United States, if U.S. policy has an effect on a country like Germany with 50 million to 60 million people, it will certainly have an impact on a country like ours with 24 million people and a much smaller capital market.
We faced those problems. The minister responded in a responsible way, and the governor of the Bank of Canada responded in a responsible way. We took that pressure, partially in interest rates-our interest rates did not go as high as those in the United States-in order to protect Canadians from even higher interest rates. But the price we paid was a reduction in the value of our currency from 87.5 cents to 83.5 cents, which I believe is today's value. Our dollar has dropped as low as 82.5 cents. To me, that is a clear indication the government understands the monetary system and that it is working in a balanced way to try to avoid the excesses which would be foisted upon us by hon. members opposite.
We have heard hon. members opposite say, "Drop the interest rate. Unilaterally keep interest rates 2 per cent, 3 per cent or 4 per cent below where they are now." That would be possible. There is no doubt that if you went stark raving mad, you could do that but consequently the value of the currency would drop like a rock. Once the public's confidence in the currency of a country is shattered, not only would you get a reduction in the value of the currency reflecting the economic situation, but you would get a reduction in the value of the currency caused by a serious financial panic in the country. That is not rational. It is not good economic policy. It is certainly not a policy that would be followed, was going to be or ever will be followed, by this government.
We hear comments from hon. members opposite that there is no development policy or economic policy which has coherence. I say that is not true at all. If we look at the budget figures we find there is a massive increase in 1981-1982 in expenditures by this government for economic development. The increase for economic development is 22 per cent. If we look at energy development, we find that expenditures for energy development will increase from $3 billion to $4 billion a year between now and 1983-1984.
If oil import compensation payments were taken out we would find energy and economic development expenditures would increase from $6.9 billion in 1980-1981 to more than $13 billion in 1983-1984. That is a massive increase in economic development funding.
We have also put in place a policy for assisting adjustment in manpower training. Clearly the government understands the difficulties. Clearly the government has put forward a rational and reasoned economic policy to deal with those difficulties.
What members of the opposition fail to understand is that one has to follow a balanced approach, one has to follow a consistent approach. Therefore one cannot devote all of the energies and resources of the government to dealing with problems in one particular area today and then shift those resources to dealing with another area tomorrow. That is what we hear from the opposition day after day. Today we hear,
"We want more expenditures; more things to help people." Tomorrow we will hear, "Forget the people, we want more things now to help increase research and development, increase industrial development, increase energy development," and so on. The following day we hear that Draconian policies are wanted to get interest rates down, among other things. It is totally inconsistent. If hon. members are honest and listening closely today, they will see that the policy prescriptions and discussions which have been put forward are the right ones.
The hon. member for Calgary Centre did not put forth any policy alternatives. He just complained bitterly about what the government was doing. We find in fact there have been no policy alternatives put forward. There has not been a fair and rational analysis of the government's economic policy, which I am convinced is the right policy.
If I might close on one note. There has been a suggestion by the hon. member for Calgary Centre that the National Energy Program is the sole and total cause of a mass exodus of oil rigs from western Canada. The hon. member for Calgary Centre should once and for all come clean. The facts of that issue are clear. They are not as told by the hon. member for Calgary Centre. In fact an oversupply of rigs was generated over the past two to three years. Gas is found in most of the holes drilled in the west. There is now a glut of gas and no hope in the near future of either domestic or foreign markets for that gas. Small producers cannot shut in that gas and sit on it. They have to sell it. If they cannot sell it, which is the market situation, why drill for it?
The other fact is that the United States has gone to world prices for oil. If hon. members opposite want us to go to world prices for oil, they should say so. That is not what they said in the past. By keeping our price below the world price, oil exploration and development in the United States is much more profitable. That is why the rigs have moved out of the country. That is being realized and admitted now in the press, in the west, and by the oil industry. The truth is finally starting to come out that it is not the big, bad NEP that is causing all the problems.
You have indicated, Mr. Speaker, that my time is up. I think I have been able to show a few things today. One is that the government understands the situation we are in presently. We have a coherent and consistent policy for dealing with that. There has been an awful lot of hokum coming from the other side of the House for the last four to five months. I hope at some time they will come to their senses and it will stop.

However, I maintain that the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and his parliamentary secretary should go through every speech to find any essence they can grab onto in order to make this a better country.
That may get us out of the economic dilemma which is crucifying our youth, senior citizens, low and middle income earners, and the balance of the economy. The only economic development I have seen come forward from this dilapidated government is a bailout for Chrysler and Massey which may cost the taxpayers of this country hundreds of millions of dollars.
There was a spending spree which will cost the taxpayers between half and three quarters of a billion dollars more than PetroFina was worth. It will not add one cupful of oil to our reserves, which are rapidly disappearing. Perhaps the government will justify the price of Petrofina by suddenly putting the price of crude oil in Canada up to world prices. Ministers will then say they are heroes, that it was worth $120 a share. That is an expensive lesson for this country.
Next week marks the first week of reduction in production in Alberta and the commencement of an additional billion dollars expenditure per year for foreign oil. This is all brought about due to the total lack of communication and co-operation of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde).
Economic Policies
The above-mentioned comments refer to bailouts, buyouts and sellouts. It will cost the taxpayers of this country $3 billion this year for this great budget. The minister talks about a 22 per cent increase. I have not worked it out, but it will be much more. What benefit are we in this country getting directly? It is time that the country stopped being fearful of plagiarism and found out how West Germany and Japan accepted world oil prices and overcame the economic disadvantages. The government continually says we cannot afford 75 per cent of world prices. Ministers should visit Japan and review the research and development in that country provided by direct grants and by tax incentives. They should send people to Texas to see the boom created by a sensible and fair energy program, both by the Democratic and Republican parties.
The government should study the American small business act which provides for reduced interest rates early in a company's origination or expansion. They do not refer to small business as a company requiring $100,000 to $500,000. They go as high as $25 million, and refer to corporations with 2,000 employees. The Americans have faced economic reality. Business today is larger than we realize it is. It must be larger in order to compete successfully in the 1980s.
Our alternative is pretty pathetic, a $100,000 guaranteed loan at one per cent over prime which works out to about 20 per cent at today's rates, or a $500,000 debenture which cannot be deducted for income tax purposes. The great Federal Business Development Bank charges 2 per cent over prime, which currently costs borrowers 20 per cent. Who can afford a 20 per cent loan on debt in this day and age?
Instead of all these Mickey Mouse plans the government should have put up guarantees to the chartered banks and subsidized interest loans. Say the interest rate is 20 per cent; the government would provide a 10 per cent subsidy to get the effective interest rate down to 10 per cent.
Assume they pay that 10 per cent directly to the banks and assume that there is a 20 per cent failure of the money that is guaranteed by the banks, which is very high. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I seem to be put in this position quite frequently. When we were interrupted for the supper hour, 1 was making a concrete suggestion. The minister said we never come up with any concrete suggestions. I would like just to repeat it.
What I was getting at was that this government has used $3 billion of taxpayers' money on the various programs it has undertaken. My proposal, very simply, is that we look at the small business act in the United States. In the United States loans are guaranteed through the chartered banks. For example, the interest rate would be reduced on small business loans by 10 per cent. In effect, a 20 per cent loan would be a 10 per cent loan. Let us assume that there is a 20 per cent failure factor with respect to these loans, so we have to write off another potential $2 billion of what we are providing. Under this scheme the government could have spent $3 billion guaranteeing $10 billion to chartered banks to help small entrepreneur Canadians to create labour, reduce unemployment and create industrialization in order to take this country from being a supplier of raw materials, which we have been since the beginning of time, to being a processor and manufacturer of finished products. This would still cost $3 billion, and I think it would be a much better way of spending our money.
It would also recover its potential cost from corporate taxes, income taxes and sales taxes, and it would give the country the opportunity to make its citizens proud, productive people. They are ashamed now. They are not as productive as their neighbours. They would like to be more productive and, by putting money into investment in manufacturing, they become more productive.
With respect to inflation, I hope with the new leader at the helm of our neighbour we might benefit from some rub-off. If we do not, then we will face not only an energy crisis by 1985 but also an inflationary crisis which will erode all the basic values upon which this country was built. We will require wheelbarrows to carry our money and bicycles for transportation because we will not be able to afford to buy cars from countries with sound currencies. They will be too expensive, and we will not even have the fuel with which to run them. Are we to face the same crisis Germany faced in the 1920s and China faced several times in the first half of this century? It is time for us to get up off our backsides and develop a sound and practical economic and industrial policy to encourage Canadians to get away from what the minister said. He said that Canadians are a discouraged group right now. Canadians should be encouraged to become a successful industrial nation, to use our huge supply of natural resources, to process them and manufacture them and create unparalleled employment and pride in our country.
The greatest fear I currently have is for our youth. I have five children. We hear about makeshift give-away programs created by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy). Some last for three months and some last for nine
months, but they do not equip youth with any benefit which will help them in future employment beyond the period a particular program lasts. We must develop long-term apprenticeship programs which permit youth to develop skills using modern technology which will enhance the productivity of Canadians in the future.
What action are we taking to assist our senior citizens? Why must we be the judges who say that a productive Canadian must retire at the magic age of 65? Let us consider the mortality rate of those gentlemen-particularly gentlemen- who retire at age 65. How many deaths are caused by boredom after energetic, useful and productive lives in the labour force? Are we addressing the erosion of their lifestyle, or have we stuck our heads in the sand hoping the problem will go away? It will not go away.
We must control government. We must get our budget into balance and bring inflation under control. We must do more than just wrestle inflation to the ground, which is the argument we have heard from the other side.
Every time I hear about a regional grant, I think regional grants are a great idea, but all the money just flows back into the two central provinces. It does not help the provinces where the money is spent. We must reassess the regional granting system. Grants should be given to the regions to develop industries which are most suited because of the proximity of raw materials, convenience to the market or the adaptability of the labour force. We must allow the regions to develop their own industries rather than industries being imposed upon them by a group of bureaucrats in Ottawa.
The government does not acknowledge that this country is made up of many different peoples from different regions with different needs and lifestyles. This should be acknowledged by the centralist government in Ottawa. They should adapt programs in conjunction with the regions, rather than subjecting the regions to ones imposed by unitary government.
The government talks about Canadianization programs. Very clearly they are nationalization programs. Is this Russia? Are those the goals we are reaching for? Does nationalizing by paying millions of dollars out of the country increase employment? Does it bring more income tax back into the country? What about corporation and sales taxes? Could it simply be a method of acquiring successful tax-paying corporations and of turning them into bungling Crown corporations run by unsuccessful Liberal candidates and unemployed friends of the party?
The truth is that Crown corporations do not work and have not worked in the past. The president and chairman of Petrofina indicated that he would not stay with the corporation. The incentive to management, owners and labour is removed. This is what is disruptive about Crown corporations.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to read into the record the motion we are discussing. The following motion was put forward by the Conservative Party:
That this House condemns the government for its failure to introduce economic policies that would restore the economy to its full potential and give Canadians confidence in their future.
This motion is couched in the most broad and obscure language; it is singularly lacking in specifics. There are no specific criticisms and no constructive or positive solutions. One must assume that the opposition, despite its rhetoric, endorses our policy because it cannot come up with anything better.
The fact is that the Canadian economy, in common with nearly every industrial country of the OECD, has undergone a period of slow growth. However, on balance the record will show that Canada has done much better than nearly all other major countries of the industrialized western world. The record is much more credible than the doom and gloom assumptions inherent in this motion.
Canada had a rather small growth, as measured by the real GNP, in 1980. This is not surprising, in view of the fact that the United States also underwent a brief, but sharp, recession in 1980 which saw a decline in real output in that country. In fact, according to the latest OECD Economic Outlook report, the four major European countries of Germany, France, United Kingdom and Italy averaged a 1.25 per cent decline in real national output in 1980. The same report suggested that our recovery in real output this year, although modest, will be better than in any other major western country, with the exception of Japan. We all know that the quality of life in Japan, where one must pay $75 for a steak dinner, would not be acceptable in Canada. If we take the entire decade from 1969 to 1979, we find that the growth of real output in Canada averaged 4.25 per cent per year. This was a record growth among all major OECD countries, second only to that of Japan.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Who was in power during that time?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. member, for 90 per cent of that time it was the Liberal government.
Compared with the United States, Canada has been at least a full percentage point a year ahead in terms of economic growth over the past decade. Attaining one's full potential is not difficult when one's major trading partners are faring relatively well. However, it is difficult in the short-term if
Economic Policies
one's trading partners are undergoing a recession. After all, Canada is one of the major trading countries of the world. Germany is the only country in the entire world which has both a larger population than Canada and larger per capita exports or imports.
We hear very little from the opposition regarding Canada's record of performance in international trade. It is not often that Canada records a trade surplus of some $8 billion, despite the recession in the United States. Two thirds of the increase in Canada's exports last year were to countries other than the United States. The increase in our exports to non-American countries more than paid for our entire increase in merchandise imports. Our share of exports going to the United States last year of 63.4 per cent was the lowest since 1966. Our share of exports going to EEC countries other than the United Kingdom was the largest during the last decade, at 8.3 per cent. These figures indicate that we are broadening and diversifying our trade and that we are less dependent on a single trading partner, particularly the United States.
Our current account surplus last year in relation to our total GNP was the best since 1974. One used to hear opposition members belabour the fact that Canada's current account deficit was the largest among OECD countries. Why do we not hear them acknowledge the fact that it is now among the best? The latest OECD Economic Outlook in December, 1980, estimated that the total OECD deficit would be in excess of $73 billion, with Germany, Japan, France and Italy all recording higher current account deficits than Canada.
While much has been said in the media regarding the exchange rate of the Canadian dollar vis-a-vis the United States dollar, comparatively little has been heard about the fact that both Canadian and United States currencies have gone up sharply in recent months as against most of the major European currencies.
In recent years our underlying competitive position has definitely improved both at home and abroad. We are benefiting from a much more competitive Canadian dollar. Our unit labour costs in manufacturing have gone up comparatively less than in nearly all major industrial countries of the western world. Coupled with substantially lower energy costs and with net export positions in food, forest products, mineral products and energy, Canada can look to the future with more confidence than any other country of the free world.
Our record of performance as far as job creation is concerned has been consistently at the very top among western OECD countries. It is not often recognized by the opposition that we are one of the few major OECD countries to show increases in manufacturing employment. In 1979 the increase in Canadian manufacturing employment was 115,000, or 5.9 per cent. Even in 1980 there was an increase in employment in manufacturing of some 37,000, or 1.8 per cent, despite the recession in the U.S. If we look at the record of manufacturing employment in recent years of some of the major industrial countries, we find that there has been an absolute decline in manufacturing employment in countries such as Japan, Ger-

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies
many, Australia, France, The Netherlands, Norway and Sweden, and I could go on.
In broader and more general terms, Canada's record of employment creation, even in the midst of a so-called recession, has been the best in the western world. In the last three years a total of over one million additional jobs were created in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Not in the private sector.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
The opposition is pointing out that Canada had a year of no growth for the first time since 1954. They should be pointing out as well that this is the so-called recession and that we added close to 300,000 persons to the employment rolls.
This government's record of performance on unemployment deserves some comment. The opposition used to insist that Canada's jobless rate was the highest of the OECD countries. However, despite that so-called recession in 1980, the unemployment rate in Canada did not increase. It remained at the same level as in 1979. More importantly, it actually declined on a seasonally adjusted rate as the year progressed. Our most recent unemployment rate of 7.3 per cent was the lowest monthly rate in the past 12 months. Despite the fact that Canada's labour force continues to grow faster than in any other major country of the OECD, current unemployment rates in this country are lower than in the United Kingdom and in Italy. They are now comparable with those of France and The Netherlands, which have stagnant labour forces or no unemployment growth.
The U.S., which only a short while ago had a lower unemployment rate than Canada, has now caught up with us. Its unemployment rate is now equal to ours. But its record on total employment and manufacturing employment gains do not compare with ours. We have done a much better job in terms of creating jobs than has the United States. It is fair to say that the policies of other countries have scarcely come near to the policies which this Canadian government has proved to be more effective in the past decade.
Let us turn now to the problem of inflation. To most people in Canada inflation is the number one problem we face. We find that it, too, is not confined to our country but that it afflicts every major industrial country of the world. It is true that the consumer price index in Canada increased by 10.1 per cent in the calendar year 1980. However, the OECD reports that the average rate of inflation went up by 11.5 per cent in four major European countries last year. It also points out that the consumer price index in the United States last year rose by 12.4 per cent, following a 13.3 per cent rise in 1979. Canada has fared much better than the United States in dealing with inflation.
Much has been made of the fact that the Canadian consumer price index rose by 12 per cent between January, 1980 and January, 1981. The fact is that energy prices, which increased by an average of under 10 per cent in both 1978 and 1979, increased by 16 per cent in 1980. Moreover, energy prices in
the most recent 12-month period increased by 25 per cent in Canada, with the increase in fuel and gasoline prices being even higher than that. Thus, it is strange to hear criticism from the opposition that we are not moving our domestic prices of energy up fast enough to close the gap with world prices. And at the same time the opposition belabours the rise in inflation. They cannot have it both ways. If we accelerate sharply the pace of energy price increases, it follows that we must witness an escalation in the rate of inflation, which carries with it high interest rates. In turn, high energy costs become imbedded in the cost of producing food, tractor and combine costs, the price of fertilization, the cost of processing, transportation, communications, clothing and other elements of the cost of living. It is inconsistent and misleading to pretend that we can fully absorb in a painless fashion increases in energy prices, which are two to three times as fast as the underlying rate of inflation, without inflation being exacerbated, as the Conservatives would like us to believe.
In summary, Canadians can comfort themselves that while we are obviously not able to realize our full potential in the short run, because of international inflation and oil shortages, the Canadian economy is faring much better than that in any other major country of the western world. There are no quick fix cures for the inflation and slow growth which afflict all countries of the industrial world. The performance of the Canadian economy is most commendable in relative terms. Given our wealth of human and natural resources and our high technology, we can look forward with confidence to the medium and the long-term future.
There is growing evidence that in terms of growth the Canadian economy in recent months may have turned the corner. The growth in the Canadian economy in the second half of last year was appreciably faster than in the first half. Moreover, there has been a definite upturn in recent months in the newly published Canadian Composite Leading Indicator.
It would appear that Canadians have more faith than their U.S. counterparts that inflation can be brought under control. Personal savings in Canada, which reflect faith in bringing inflation under control, in recent years have been consistently higher than in the United States, about 10 per cent versus 5 per cent. The speculative bubble which has been present with respect to gold, silver and other commodities has burst. Wage rates, which have kept up with the consumer price index, have been relatively restrained for some time now. All in all, Canadians can look beyond the immediate problems to the medium and long term with confidence.
Before closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise two concerns that I see with respect to our national economy. The first is that we must reach a speedy agreement on oil pricing to reduce uncertainty in the business community and to reduce the uncertainty of the people of Canada.
