speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
The second is that the doom and gloom prophecies and criticisms which come from the Conservative Party
February 24, 1981

create uncertainty in the business community and in the people of Canada. There is not much we can do about that.
The federal government has shown flexibility with regard to oil price agreements. It is up to the Premier of Alberta to recognize that we cannot go on any longer without an oil pricing agreement. He must recognize that we cannot go to world prices and that Canada as a whole cannot suffer increased inflation, increased unemployment and lack of energy security in order to allow Peter Lougheed to build his Alberta Heritage Fund.
There are also regional diversities in the economy of our country. This government deals with them. We have adjusted our industrial strategy so that we can deal with the problem of the west having a booming economy while the economies of Ontario, Quebec and the maritimes are slowing down. We also have DREE programs and equalization grants to support our social programs which are so important.
I think it is important to recognize that Canada has developed a national economic policy, in conjunction with a national energy policy, that provides a climate for the full development of our economic potential. I support this government's position right down the line.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang), who just finished his remarks.
I cannot help but comment on some of the things he said. Everyone starts out by comparing our economy to others around the world and saying that we have done well in relative terms. The point must be made that other countries are not as fortunate in their physical and human resources as we are. Surely the only legitimate comparison is with our own potential.
For those hon. members from Quebec who follow hockey, I would point out that the Montreal Canadiens do not play in a league with the Sherbrooke Beavers; they play in their own league. Surely that is the kind of comparison we should make of our ability to perform in the sphere of economics. We should be talking about our own potential rather than comparing ourselves to countries less fortunate in physical and human resources.
Two or three weeks ago, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) spoke in this House and told us that on one of his business trips to Hong Kong some businessmen had remarked on the opportunities and resources that Canada has, and said they could not understand how we managed to mess things up so badly.
This afternoon the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) spoke of an unexpected strong recovery and referred to a 1.7 per cent annual growth. I do not know how anyone could regard a growth of 1.7 per cent as unexpected. He pointed out that employment continues to rise but he did not mention that
Economic Policies
unemployment is also rising. For the first time in this country the total number of people who are out of the marketplace and looking for work is over one million. Hon. members opposite should be consistent, and when they speak of the rise in employment they should also speak of unemployment as a percentage of the total work force. Otherwise we only get half the story.
The Minister of Finance also spoke of an $ 11 billion trade surplus which he claimed was close to being cancelled by the deficit in the non-merchandise account.
I have some graphs here that were prepared by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington). We all recognize the valuable work he has done on behalf of the business community of this country. They show that the monthly trade balance in food products, which are basically raw material, is on the increase. Exports of crude materials such as coal and products which do not have value added to them, are on the increase. Exports of semi-manufactured products are on the increase. When it comes to manufactured goods, however, there was an $11 billion deficit in 1977, a $12.2 billion deficit in 1978 and a $17.2 billion deficit in 1979. When we import manufactured goods, we import jobs, but when we export raw material we export jobs. In 1980 the deficit in manufactured goods was close to $18 billion. When we talk about trade surpluses, therefore, we should remember that the surplus is basically in raw materials. The things that create jobs and wealth for our citizens are end products, but in this category the graph zooms down to the basement. If we could have manufactured the $18 billion worth of end products that we imported last year, 350,000 jobs would have been created in this country.
That is the kind of thing we would like this government to do. We realize it cannot do everything and that things cannot be changed overnight but we must move to correct this horrendous balance of payments deficit in the manufacturing sector. We cannot ignore it or pretend, as the minister did, that we have a trade surplus of $11 billion, without pointing out where that surplus is. We cannot address the problem unless we recognize it.
The Minister of Finance is not in his place this evening. He was scheduled to appear at a meeting of the finance committee this evening to discuss Bill C-59, the borrowing authority bill. Hon. members will remember that the government introduced closure in order to get it to committee in a hurry. I understand that no notice was given of cancellation of the committee meeting and there was no meeting of the steering committee. A notice was sent to the offices of members of the committee that it would not meet this evening. The excuse given was that the minister would be in the House listening to our expressions of concern about the Canadian economy. The minister is not only silent, he is contemptuous. If he is not going to be in the House tonight, surely he could have at least gone to the finance committee meeting. The very able Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Evans) is in the House, and I am pleased to see him. Surely the minister should have had the courtesy to come to the House after cancelling the committee meeting.

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies
This afternoon the parliamentary secretary covered many aspects of the Canadian economy in his speech. At one point he spoke of the opposition being intellectually honest and academically correct. I should like to remind him of his appearance at the finance committee in December, 1979, when the subject was interest rates, and quote from the proceedings of that committee to illustrate how he has been intellectually honest and academically correct, consistent and coherent, as he said in his speech. I should like to draw attention to some of the things he said when he was outside the government and to point to some of the policies this government is pursuing at the present time.
Speaking of the Bank of Canada, he said on December 11, 1979, as reported at page 21:14 of the committee proceedings:
When the chips are down, the bank cannot be relied upon to maintain its control over the money supply; as a result, would you agree that this should result in a removal of discretionary authority from the bank, and a directive, as you said, to maintain control over the monetary aggregates only?
The committee was considering a method of controlling the money supply as a means of regulating the inflation rate. He continued:
And I would go one step further, as I have in the past in this committee, and ask you if that would imply to you that the bank be given a directive to allow both interest rates and the exchange rate to find their own level in the marketplace without outside intervention.
The question under consideration was that of the Bank of Canada interfering in the marketplace to regulate the interest rate or the value of the Canadian dollar. When he was in opposition, the parliamentary secretary advocated that the money supply be set and the market allowed to determine the interest rate and the value of the dollar.
We know that the Bank of Canada regularly interferes in the marketplace-every Thursday at the auction-to do what it can to regulate the value of the Canadian dollar. When the parliamentary secretary talks about being coherent and consistent, I would urge him to set an example, which is not evident in some of the things he has said at the finance committee and some of the things he now supports as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. If the government wants to urge members on this side of the House to be coherent and consistent, I should like the parliamentary secretary to do the same.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has miraculously appeared. I hope he remains to listen to what I have to say. This afternoon, when he was congratulating himself on the performance of the Canadian economy, I was afraid that he might get a sore arm from patting himself on the back. Indeed, I was about to suggest that the House should send him a bottle of liniment to use on his arm so that it would not get any worse. However, he has returned to the Chamber and I am glad.
I should like to turn now to some 'of the things that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said. The government insists that we be consistent and coherent in all we say, but we
all remember the occasion two or three years ago when, in a year-end review, the Prime Minister said we would have to accept more government interference in the marketplace, because a free market economy obviously does not work. In answer to a question put two or three weeks ago, the Minister of Finance said that the government still believes in the market economy, in the market approach. I would urge that the government get its own act together and decide what is consistent and coherent as far as its policy is concerned.
Let me talk a little about an area that I come from, and that is western Canada, and relate it to grain movement in particular. We all know that there are many problems associated with the grain transportation business in western Canada. There have been many positions advocated as to how to correct this problem. What I find rather unfortunate-I want to pick a word here that is not too hard on the government-is that the government itself cannot get its own act together to decide what kind of approach it wants to take to this problem.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: How about "stupid"?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
We have the minister in the other place responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board saying he does not want anything done with the statutory rate problem. We have the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) saying, in a speech given in Edmonton some two weeks ago, that he would like to see the matter resolved within the current crop year, which would mean that there would be a solution to it by August 1, 1981. We had the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) saying that he would like to refer the matter-or is trying to get a position through cabinet whereby the matter would be referred-back to the Canadian farmer through a position paper. We also have the minister responsible for economic development in the other place saying he does not want anything done until there is a chance to do some kind of study on the CPR and the land grants that it had, and whether those kinds of revenues from the land should be included in the revenues that the railroads are claiming against other things besides grain movement.
So, we have four ministers of the Crown taking different positions. I find this very unfortunate, because what has happened in the past two to three years, is that farm groups have come together and established a negotiating position. I might add that when you have several farm groups representing large numbers of farmers in western Canada coming together and agreeing on a position to take to the government, it is a position that is arrived at with a considerable amount of soul-searching, and yet that is what has gone on in western Canada, and that is the position that farm leaders have taken.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said here in the House, some two weeks ago, that he does not want to move on the statutory rate issue until the farm community has established its position. I find that, again, to be a very unfortunate statement because if the farm community was being irresponsible, I can simply say that our position is unified. We want
February 24, 1981

the government to assume all of the additional costs between the compensatory rate and the statutory rate, and that should be paid to the railways by the federal government, which would be a further drain on the federal treasury.
The farm groups in western Canada have not taken this position, although I think it would be very easy for them to do, and it would be a unified position, and they could take it to the Prime Minister, who says he wants to have a unified position presented to him. It would be very easy for the farm groups to simply get together and say, "We want the federal government to totally fund the difference between the statutory rate and the Crow rate," and yet the farm community has not done this. They have taken a responsible position, yet the Prime Minister castigates them because they do not have a unified position, and he is not going to move on it until they do.
I might add that it is not simply a problem for western Canada, as I pointed out in this House several times before. It is a major problem which affects all of Canada. It would help us in our foreign exchange earnings and help to add to the $11 billion surplus which, as the minister correctly pointed out, Canada had in its trading accounts. It would add to that. As a result, it would add to the value of our dollar. It would decrease the pressure on our interest rates and thus, we hope, lower the interest rate. It would help the manufacturing industry in eastern Canada, and, it would help Massey-Fergu-son and Chrysler, so that presumably those companies could find themselves in a better financial position.
This is what I find to be inconsistent as far as this government is concerned. Again, I have to castigate them for standing up and simply saying that we cannot have it both ways. I am not asking for additional government expenditures, and at the same time expecting the government to go ahead and decrease its deficit. Nothing I have said this evening has pointed in both directions at the same time.
The government can do one other thing which would not in the least involve an increase in its expenditures and would show benefits as far as the economy is concerned. For a brief time, when my party was in power, we appointed a grain transportation co-ordinator to look after grain movement in western Canada. This is a position which has been long advocated by all parties in the House. The position was filled in October of 1979 by Dr. Hugh Horner, a former member of this House. He resigned from that position in October of this year, and that position has not yet been filled by the Minister of Transport. I find this unfortunate, because we all know that we have limited transportation capabilities in western Canada, and the co-ordinator was doing an excellent job of getting the best out of our grain transportation system. Most of the people to whom I have talked thought that he had done a very good job in terms of co-ordinating grain movement. This is a position that is now vacant.
We have an acting director of the grain transportation authority in western Canada. We have several people assembled from industry across Canada who have been on loan to the grain transportation authority, people from the grain companies, from the transportation companies. They are rapidly
Economic Policies
losing morale, and the information I have is that a lot of them will be thinking very seriously about resigning before the start of the spring planting season in western Canada. If we lose these people whom industry has loaned to the grain transportation authority, the whole grain transportation authority is in danger of collapsing. This is a responsibility of the federal government, and I would urge the federal government to go ahead and assume its responsibility. Again, it would not cost the federal treasury any additional money. The position is in place, and simply to let it die by default by not appointing a new co-ordinator, to my way of thinking, is a shame, because it is one way of making maximum use of the limited number of transportation facilities we have in western Canada.
I would like to point out another area in which I have concerns. When the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski) was minister of transport, he made no bones about establishing the goal of increasing our exports of grain by some 20 per cent over the just-concluded crop year. We have not heard anything in terms of a target like that.
Let me back up. The target was to increase our capabilities, to export grain by 20 per cent so that by the year 1985 we would be exporting 30 million tons of grain. He came very close to increasing the amount of exports that we had by 20 per cent, and without the unfortunate accident in Vancouver in which the Second Narrows Bridge collapsed we would have reached it during 1979-80.
So far as I am aware, the government has not presently announced any intentions of what their target will be for increasing the amount of exports. Again, this would help our economy. It would help, as I said previously, our ability to foreign exchange around the world, because we know that grain is certainly going to be in demand around the world. Anybody you talk to who is in the grain export business knows that our grain will be sold if we get to export position.
As I pointed out, there are a couple of areas in which the government can do without spending additional amounts of money. It would help the government to earn more taxes, thus increasing the revenue base from which the government operates. At the same, it would not increase government expenditures.
In addition, we heard the western development fund announced in the Speech from the Throne. This is a commitment of money that is apparently made to western Canada. Some of us have made suggestions to the government as to how this money should be spent. We have suggested that it be spent on infrastructing on roads, on upgrading railroads, and things of that nature that will be an investment and will show a return as a result of that part of the country being able to produce more.
I understand, from the conversations that I have had with some of the members opposite, that there have really been no guidelines set as to how this western development fund would be used. There is an area that the government could pursue without committing any additional money, and thereby increasing the government deficit. I would urge the government to get on with setting the guidelines for how the western

Economic Policies
development fund will be used so that we can proceed to use this money to help us generate more jobs and more economic activity in the country.
In the time remaining I would like to speak briefly about the small business community. As some of you know, the small business community-depending on whether you look at new jobs or the total jobs in the small business sector-accounts for roughly 50 per cent of the jobs in Canada. One of the things we tried to impress on the minister when we talked about the Small Business Development Bond is that it should be extended past the end of the current year, and that it should also be extended to businesses that are unincorporated. I have also had conversations with the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres), and I appreciate the opportunity I have had to speak to him. Any of the times that I have talked to them, they have pointed out that it is a very expensive program, and that it would be hard to justify extending the Small Business Development Bond past March 31, 1981.
Recently I received some information from the Canadian Federation of Independent Business which shows that the amount of money required to create a job under the Small Business Development Bond-to create jobs, not to maintain jobs, which is another aspect-is lower than for some of the other programs. For instance, the Canadian Federation for Independent Business estimates that it would cost $5,600 to create a job under the Small Business Development Bond concept. Under the Regional Development Incentive Program, the cost was $8,400. The Canada Works is roughly equivalent to the Small Business Development Bond. In the local employment assistance programs it costs $7,000 to create each job. I would urge the minister to have another look at the Small Business Development Bond. What appeals to me and to the small business community about it is that there is no paper work involved. We all know of the paper burden. We all know of the work which has been done by the office of paper burden reduction. I have to congratulate the minister on this. I think the office has done a good job and it is generally recognized that that office has done a lot to eliminate paper work which is a real headache for many small businesses.
So far I have just talked about the cost to the government to create a job in terms of lost tax revenue. It says nothing about the kinds of jobs that will be maintained. The Small Business Development Bond is of the most benefit to those businesses that are not taxable. In the main it will serve to keep those people in business. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business estimated they would create 36,000 jobs by a loss to government of $1.25 billion. I asked the CFIB for a figure, and I asked them if they had done any work on their models to show how many jobs would be saved if everybody who made use of the Small Business Development Bond were in a loss position or in a non-taxable position. The estimate was 63,000 jobs. Therefore it seems to me you could look at a considerably lower figure than $5,600.
If we look at the Small Business Development Bond, not only in terms of the additional jobs it would create but also in terms of jobs it would save you would find that the people who would benefit the most from it are those in a loss position, and a figure considerably lower than $5,600 to create one job would result. Even now $5,600 compares very favourably to the other costs of creating jobs under other government programs. As I said, the beauty of it is there is no paper work.
I hope that I have pointed out to the government that there are many things we have said on this side consistent with a lower deficit and increased economic activity which, in the long run, will generate more taxes for the government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) who led off our party in this debate began his speech by telling us that when he went home his constituents greeted him with the simple question: "Good God, what are you people doing in Ottawa?" I suppose members will not be surprised if I say that is precisely the question I am asked whenever I am home on weekends.
Last year the cost of living went up by 12 per cent. For food consumed at home, it went up by over 13 per cent. For fuel and utilities, the cost of living went up over 21 per cent. Therefore, it is not surprising people complain and wonder what they are going to do. It is not surprising that a Conservative economist, Michael Manford, of Merrill Lynch Royal Securities Ltd., is quoted in today's The Globe and Mail as saying that inflation in Canada in the next year will get worse rather than better. It is not surprising that workers who are still fortunate enough to have jobs, particularly when they belong to unions and have some bargaining power, are now beginning to demand and are trying to get double-digit wage increases. Workers need an increase of more than 10 per cent just to try to keep their standard of living where it was last year.
It was disturbing, to say the least, to read the speech given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) yesterday to the Canadian Club. In part it read:
The simple truth is that as a nation, we are entitled only to what we can produce. We are entitled to our gross national product-to nothing more, to nothing less-and rising entitlements can only be legitimized through increased economic growth.
Last year's economic growth was less than 2 per cent. It will probably be less than 2 per cent this year. If that is all ordinary citizens can look forward to, then the minister is saying to them that they can expect and should get a decrease in their real income of about 10 per cent. This is not what the minister is expecting of other sectors of society, those who do not work for wages and salaries. He certainly has no right to expect that kind of approach from ordinary people in this country.
Also there are concerns about unemployment. I heard the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Lang) boast about how well we are doing in Canada. I do not think we have a right to boast when according to official figures 945,000 people were unemployed in January of this year. That is 8.3 per cent of the

work force. The figure for women and young people is substantially higher than that.
The former minister of employment and immigration implied on more than one occasion that unemployment was not very serious because often it is not the primary earner who is unemployed. Nothing could be further from the truth. People in this country are very concerned. They are not only faced with the kind of unemployment now prevalent in most parts of the industrialized world; they are now frequently seeing a very disturbing phenomenon in Canada. They see plants which have been in operation for 50 or more years being closed and the people who have worked in these plants for all of their working lives losing their jobs. These plants are being closed for reasons beyond the ability of the workers to do anything about it.
Yesterday morning before I came to Ottawa I met with a group of workers who had worked at the Maple Leaf Mills Ltd. plant which had been in operation in Winnipeg for more than 50 years. It closed very recently. Let me illustrate what unemployment and plant closure mean to one person. This illustration could be duplicated hundreds and thousands of times across Canada, but the situation in Winnipeg is not nearly as serious as that in the province of Ontario. My example concerns a woman, age 57, who worked at the Maple Leaf mills for 35 years. Just before the plant closed she was earning $8.61 an hour or about $344 a week. When the plant closed, this woman was laid off. At age 57, it is very unlikely she will ever get a job again, certainly not one that would pay her the kind of money she was earning. She worked in a unionized mill. The union contract had a clause in it about severance pay, so this woman will receive full pay for the next 35 weeks. In other words, she will receive 35 weeks of severance pay which works out to about $12,000. Also she will receive almost a full year of unemployment insurance benefits. However, after that she will be in real trouble because the mill did not have a good pension plan. She will get $81 a month until she reaches age 65. How is that woman to manage? How are many of the people who are being laid off to manage? Nevertheless, the minister indicated that workers in this country cannot expect any more in increased pay than the increase in productivity.
I have pointed out how wrong the minister was to have suggested that, but if he really believed it, he should have taken steps to see that kind of approach applied across the board to all sectors of our society. The hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap talked about that this afternoon. While the minister has been telling the Canadian people to lower their expectations, the government never applied that kind of thinking to the business community in this country.
According to the business section of yesterday's Globe and Mail, the banks in this country increased their assets in the last year by 22.7 per cent; the Royal Bank, 22.1 per cent, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, 20 per cent; Bank of Montreal, 30.3 per cent; Bank of Nova Scotia, 25.9 per cent and Toronto-Dominion Bank, 23.4 per cent. Therefore, we are
Economic Policies
not talking about small impoverished corporations but the largest and richest corporations in this country.
When we look at their profits, we see they are in the hundreds of millions of dollars. In 1980, the Royal Bank increased its profits after taxes by 21 per cent from $270 million to $327 million, the Bank of Montreal by 15.1 per cent to $263 million, the Toronto-Dominion Bank by 14.5 per cent to $121 million and the Bank of Nova Scotia by 22.3 per cent to $221 million.
The oil companies have gone on strike. When a group of workers in this country goes on strike, immediately we see editorials in newspapers and demands in Parliament and the legislatures that something be done to stop the strike because it creates difficulties for the people. The oil companies, among the richest corporations in this country, have gone on strike. They have refused to invest in Canada and are cutting back on exploration. Why? They are not making enough profits. The figures show that is untrue, that it is a lie.
The figures are very clear. In 1980, the profits of Imperial Oil increased by 38.3 per cent over 1979 to $682 million, Shell Canada by 37.1 per cent to $355 million, Gulf by 31.9 per cent to $380 million and Texaco by 41.5 per cent to $373 million. That is what is going on in this country, but the Minister of Finance tells the ordinary citizen of this country to cut back on his expectations. All he wants is to live the kind of life he lived in the past. He is prepared to work and do his share.
What did the minister say in his speech in Montreal? He said we are in trouble because our productivity is not growing. He said:
Although we have enjoyed roughly the same rate of employment growth in the last seven years, output per worker has not only failed to increase-it has actually declined.
An editorial in some part of Canada will indicate we are not doing great because Canadian workers are not prepared to work. That is not true. If our productivity is not increasing as it was in other years, there are very clear reasons why. It is not because Canadian workers do not want to work. It is because government and industry have not prepared for the kind of society in which we live.
We have no industrial strategy in this country. Despite all the speeches he made while in opposition, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) has not brought forward an industrial strategy. The result is that our manufacturing industries are steadily declining. In 1970, 26 per cent of the work force was engaged in manufacturing. By 1979 that figure had dropped to 19 per cent. In 1970, 21 per cent of our exports were manufactured goods. Today it is 10 per cent. In 1970, we had a $3 billion deficit in manufactured goods. In 1979 the deficit was $11.5 billion.
Our factories are not operating anywhere near capacity. Plants which were designed to operate on two shifts now work only one shift. Workers who were working five and six days a week now work three. Corporations did not use their profits in years of high profit to modernize and retool their plants and equipment.

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies
For many years the automobile industry made tremendous profits, as did the pulp and paper industry. Now they come to government cap in hand asking for help. The percentage of our labour force in the service sector is increasing every year. That sector is not as productive as the manufacturing or mining industries or the oil and gas industry which is highly mechanized and automated.
Lastly, we have the spectacle of Canadian corporations and the multinationals involved in a rash of takeovers; Thomson buying FP Publications and Hudson's Bay, CP busily trying to buy corporations in the United States and Seagrams wheeling and dealing. These takeovers do not add anything to the productive capacity of this country. This is why our productivity has not increased in recent years.
This country is and will continue to be in trouble as long as the government refuses to do what every other country in the industrialized world has done, with the exception of the United States and Canada. Government must take the lead in planning, together with industry and labour, to use human and natural resources to the fullest capacity in order to produce our food and the goods for which we have a natural advantage and compete for sales in the international markets in order to keep Canadians working.
Until the government gets involved in that kind of planning and devises the kind of industrial strategy the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce spoke about so volubly when in opposition, this country will not only continue to be in trouble but the trouble will get much worse.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roy MacLaren (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the discussion this evening centres on the goal of greater economic growth, a goal we all desire. We look for growth to be sustained over time and growth to be balanced in a regional as well as in an industrial sense.
In seeking those broad goals, we have committed ourselves as a government to reducing the deficit in our total balance of payments. Second, we have undertaken to reduce the rate of inflation. Third, we are seeking to promote employment and viable industries and to generate more exports. Fourth, of course, we want to implement those policies in a way which benefits all regions of Canada. This evening I want to say a word about broad goals in terms of the National Energy Program announced in the budget last autumn.
We seek a reduction in the current deficit in our balance of payments by eliminating, as a major goal of that program, the need for imported oil. We are also doing so through a fundamental commitment to conservation, which has been absent in Canada in the past. We are also doing so through a commitment to substitution of more plentiful forms of fuel for scarce and expensive oil. We seek also, through incentives to the industry, to bring on-stream new supplies of domestic petroleum.
As the House knows and as most Canadians know, Canada is today more than energy self-sufficient. We are, in fact, net exporters of energy. With the National Energy Program, we have set ourselves the additional goal of becoming self-sufficient in oil by 1990. Those programs will help us to correct the deficit in our balance of payments, one of the principal goals of our current economic policy.
With regard to its effects on inflation and unemployment, we have not undertaken in the National Energy Program, a cheap oil policy. However, as the national government of our country we must manage our national economy. We must protect consumers just as we must ensure producers a fair return.
I might note in this connection that in estimating the impact of inflation resulting from higher energy prices, the Economic Council of Canada recently estimated that a one dollar increase in the price of a barrel of oil will add about .5 per cent to the consumer price index. Rather than push inflation even higher, we want Canadians to pay less than world price for their oil, leaving the difference in the pockets of people rather than in the coffers of governments.
I have referred to industrial growth, and the employment that is generated from such growth, as another principal economic policy commitment of this government.
We see the energy policy and, indeed, the energy industry as principal motors of the further growth in our economy. In that connection, we have distinctly Canadian assets. We have become a leader in the technologies associated with oil sands, enhanced oil recovery, natural uranium reactors and frontier petroleum exploration, particularly in sensitive environments.
I do not need to remind the House of the commitments made in the national energy policy to major expenditures between 1980 and 1983 which will give further incentive to growth in this most dynamic segment of our total economy. Those who have consulted the National Energy Program will recognize that almost $12 billion has been allocated to a variety of activities which will bring additional growth to our economy, but growth on a basis which will promote regional balance throughout our country. We look toward equalization, the sharing of benefits and, indeed, the sharing of the costs in developing further in that most prosperous sector in our economy. But by doing so in a way which brings advantage to all regions of Canada, we are nevertheless ensuring that the principal oil-producing province, Alberta, will receive over $100 billion in revenue from petroleum during this decade.
In the National Energy Program, Canadianization is also a major element which makes for economic growth. We want to ensure that more benefits resulting from the growth of our petroleum sector go to Canadian workers and that more of the profits remain in Canada to be reinvested in our own economy.
The means of enhancing Canadian participation in our petroleum sector involves four principal methods. First, we seek to encourage companies already active in the oil and gas industries, by grants and other incentives, to become more
February 24, 1981

Canadian in ownership and control, such as in the recent case of Dome.
Second, we are encouraging Canadian companies not now active in the petroleum sector to enter the oil and gas industry.
Third, new companies which were not in place in the past are being formed. I refer, for example, to the initiatives taken by the co-operatives in Canada to enter the petroleum industry.
Fourth, the vehicle of Petro-Canada is available to play an active role in attempting, on behalf of all Canadians, to acquire outright, foreign-controlled firms. We have recently seen the example of its acquisition of Petrofina, which ensures that a fully-integrated national oil company will be operating for the benefit of all Canadians.
In giving further substance of our National Energy Program, we have consulted the private sector in order to benefit from its suggestions about how the program might best be applied. We remain determined to achieve our goals, but we remain equally flexible with respect to the ways in which we may achieve them.
The National Energy Program is one of the most comprehensive, far-reaching economic initiatives undertaken by any government in Canada in recent decades. The very size and complexity of the challenges we have faced have made necessary detailed and continuing consultation with the petroleum industry and, indeed, all those sectors of our economy affected by the program. That need was recognized from the start. It has gone forward. Several significant adjustments have resulted from consulting with the petroleum industry in the elaboration of the National Energy Program.
I wish to take a few minutes to record for those interested some of the initiatives we have recently taken. First, the industry indicated to us that a new definition of Canadian exploration expenses proposed in the budget would have had an adverse impact on the industry's ability to finance such investments. We responded in Bill C-54. It contains amendments to ensure the immediate deduction of expenses incurred in drilling dry holes, whether for development or exploratory purposes.
Favourable tax treatment will also be continued for wells drilled in frontier areas before the commencement of production. In addition, the existing treatment of drilling costs of wells which qualify for exploration expenses was extended for a further year, to the end of 1981.
Second, the industry suggested to us that the value of the incentive payments outlined in the program could be increased if investors had access to a full tax deduction for exploration and development expenses prior to fulfilling all the requirements for a grant. The rules which we first set forth were subsequently amended to accommodate the industry's suggestions.
Third, while the payment of the generous incentive grants to eligible investors would increase their available cash for
Economic Policies
petroleum investment, an accounting problem arose in the treatment of grants in their annual operating statements. A typical Canadian company receiving petroleum incentive grants might show an encouraging rise in reinvestment capacity but at the same time a discouraging external appearance of reduced income, unless the grants could be fully reflected in income from the beginning. Accordingly, the government has been working with representatives of the petroleum industry in order to explore ways in which full and favourable impact of the incentive grants may be reflected in the financial positions of companies.
Fourth, the House may recall that in recent days new rules governing the Canadian ownership requirements were announced. They result from the response of industry to an invitation from the government some time ago to discuss tentative proposals for the measurement of beneficial Canadian ownership to determine the eligibility of individual companies for incentive grants. After consultation with more than 100 corporations, individuals and associations active in the petroleum industry, significant changes were recently incorporated in the Canadian ownership rating rules.
These include a provision to deem as 100 per cent Canadian all shareholdings of less than $50,000 and with Canadian addresses. We shall enable small companies of less than $5 million in assets or $10 million in revenue to complete a short form application for their Canadian ownership measurement. Numerous other changes designed to streamline the necessarily rigorous process of establishing true Canadian ownership and grant eligibility have been made.
Fifth, there have been intensive discussions of the petroleum incentive program with industry. Those discussions resulted in a new phased-in approach to Canadian ownership targets, including the creation of a new intermediate level of incentive grants. Under the new sliding scale of targets, companies with Canadian control and at least 65 per cent Canadian ownership in 1981 will be eligible for maximum incentive grants. The minimum requirement for these grants will rise by two percentage points annually to reach 75 per cent, the goal we originally proposed for 1981.
Sixth, a new intermediate category of incentive payments will be available to Canadian-controlled companies with at least 60 per cent Canadian ownership in 1981, rising by one percentage point annually to 65 per cent by 1986. The creation of this new category of eligible companies will enable many corporations to spend more on petroleum exploration than had been previously anticipated. This will provide an attractive intermediate target for those companies with Canadian ownership of between 50 per cent and 59 per cent in 1981.
The government regarded as reasonable and creative the view of the petroleum industry that a phased-in approach would ease the pressure on Canadian capital markets enabling greater access to new equity financing by the many companies now responding to the Canadianization proposals in the National Energy Program. At the same time, oil and gas supply for the benefit of all Canadians will be enhanced by a more vigorous pace of incentive-assisted investment.

February 24, 1981
Economic Policies
The evidence is there. We have been flexible. We shall continue to be so. Ideas for making the National Energy Program more practicable and effective have been welcomed and are clearly producing results. We look for more of the same kind of reasonable, ongoing consultation as the National Energy Program is put into full effect. Co-operation is essential, for example, for the successful implementation of our ambitious off-oil or substitution program on which the total goal of Canadian oil self-sufficiency by 1990 depends so much.
The Government of Canada has clearly assumed a strong leadership role in the national energy policy. But strength should not be mistaken for inflexibility. There are those who argue that our willingness to make adjustments in the National Energy Program is beside the point. From time to time we hear from critics that although they may profess full support for our basic goals, they hasten to reject our methods as mistaken or unworkable. I submit that any examination of the National Energy Program and the particular elaborations we have brought forward will show that not only will Canadian ownership be enhanced by the program, but Canadian supply and self-sufficiency in oil will also be strengthened.

I do not understand why the more important issues of this country must be discussed on opposition days. When I return to my riding in British Columbia, those people tell me that we should not be discussing the Constitution in the House of Commons, but we should be discussing the cost of living. They do not want to hear about a charter of rights; they want to hear about a reduction in interest rates. They do not want to hear about an amending formula; they want a means to lower unemployment and create jobs.
I wonder how many members on the government benches, when they wake up in the morning, instantly think of the nuances of the Constitution which is before the House.

speechtext:
We on this side of the House and a good many members on the other side can freely admit that at the moment this country has absolutely no industrial strategy. There has been a total failure. When we think of what is going on in terms of regulatory reform in the government, when we consider the many changes which have already been made to the energy policy, we realize that there is very little communication and consultation with either business or the people of this country. Otherwise, this kind of debate could be taken up for matters which are important to the people out there, not what is important to one arrogant old man trying to go down in history, with a good many people following along behind him.
What this government does is govern by fiat, not by fairness and not by interest in what the people are doing. We heard the previous speaker talk about what in my view is the deplorable oil policy. I would like to give a couple of examples of what is, taking place in the west and what this oil policy is doing to small business in the city of Vancouver. On April 1, according to the oil policy, Canadian suppliers of heavy bunker oil will be trying to sell a product for which there will be a very insignificant market.
I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) will listen to me, since what we have is a fight between the Department of Transport, which understands a bit about this situation, the Department of Finance, which does not understand the situation, and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources which wants but will not receive those tax dollars.
The current Canadian price of Bunker C is S28.20 a barrel. The proposed price with the new tax included will be $38.59. The current Puget Sound price for Bunker C is $31. That means there will be an increase of $13.45 a barrel Canadian, or a 47 per cent increase in price. For the benefit of members opposite I should explain where Puget Sound is, since one of the officials in the Department of Finance, when questioned on the matter, asked me where it was. It is immediately south of Vancouver. 1 suggest maps be provided to the various departments so that they can find out a little bit about their own country and the neighbouring shores.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: Where is Vancouver?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
For the benefit of the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre), Vancouver is 800 miles west of Calgary.
The new tax will bring marine diesel fuels up to $53.34 a barrel. This represents an increase of $18.95, or a 55 per cent increase. What will happen when these taxes come into effect on April 1? Perhaps the government will change its mind, and all service industries will be hit, along with all hotels, restaurants, ship repair establishments and longshoremen.
February 24, 1981

I would like to give a more concrete example of what is taking place. At the present time there are 40 Polish fishing vessels off the coast of Canada. They are serviced by the Kuszuby II, a factory ship. When in Vancouver for refuelling, price changes were announced, and it left immediately for Puget Sound. The loss in taxes to the federal government was $500,000. The loss to British Columbia through provincial sales taxes was $44,000.
The Poles expressed difficulty with respect to forecasting whether to ever again enter the port of Vancouver in order to refuel. Those taxes and differences in prices are destroying the marine bunkering industry. Five companies involved will now be out of business because most of the ocean-going traffic will go south. Why? Because the Department of Transport, the Department of Finance and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources cannot sort out the situation among themselves and do not realize what they are doing to the west coast. One example of what they are doing with your energy policy-

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: "Our" energy policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
It is yours, not mine.
Another example of the kind of foul-up which is occurring, not only on the west coast but on the east coast as well, has to do with the current Canadian price for marine diesel fuel of $34.39 a barrel. The current Puget Sound price is $42.81. This government proposes to increase the price by 55 per cent. The proposed Canadian price will then be $53.34, substantially higher than the American price. The export tax will go into effect when the destination of a Canadian vessel is a foreign port, regardless of any other ports of call. We will lose 25 per cent of the jobs for seagoing and associated personnel. This does not include losses to the berthing and maintenance service industries. Smile, if you will, but bear in mind we are talking about 2,000 jobs.
Canadian vessel owners must bid for contracts in competition with U.S. companies which have access to cheaper fuel. Towing cement from Gibsons Landing, British Columbia, to Adak in the Aleutian Islands will cost a Canadian firm $58,000 more than a U.S. firm for the same contract, the same service. The reason is the government's ruddy export tax which should not be applied in this case as it is costing Canadians their jobs. It is costing the west coast a good deal and I suspect the same is true on the east coast.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: They are just jobs in British Columbia.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
They are jobs in British Columbia. I also suspect they are jobs in Halifax. When the government talks about its magnificent energy policy, it should get down to the nitty-gritty, talk to the people in business who are dealing in these areas, the small companies, the backbone of this country, which the government is destroying.
I ask the ministers responsible to look at what is happening. Any sensible person will realize that the oil export tax applied at the level it is on the west coast will destroy all kinds of jobs. I suppose this matters not to the government, since the govern-
Economic Policies
ment representatives from the west coast have not brought this to their attention.
I would like to talk about other insensibilities of this government. We have a government which is economically insensitive to what is taking place in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext: It is bad all over.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICIES
speechtext:
It is bad all over. What causes that? A government that will not address itself to issues important to Canadians.
Let us talk about some Department of Fisheries and Oceans regulations. On the west coast there are new regulations in connection with salmon sport fishing. These will damage the B.C. tourist industry substantially. They will hamper small resorts, and marine operators who cater to U.S. sport fishermen along the coast. The ban imposed by the government includes a total four-month ban on all sport fishing in the Georgia Strait beginning next December. It includes an immediate ban on downriggers and one Chinook a day limit starting April 1. Everyone is concerned with Chinook salmon on the west coast, even the sport fisherman, but there must be a better way of imposing the regulations. There must be a way that fisheries officials could consult with sport fishermen's associations to arrive at some form of ban or reduction that makes sense.
Let me give some shocking figures with respect to something else. I do not care what regulations there are on sport fishing, until the government does something, those regulations cannot be enforced. In 1948, there were 109 fisheries inspectors on the west coast and approximately 3,000 private small boats at that time. Today, at latest count, there are 204,404 rowboats, inboards, outboards, sailboats, canoes and, for all I know, some tubs as well. How many fisheries inspectors does it take to handle some 204,000 sports fishermen?
In 1948 there were 109, and in 1981 there are 120. That shows a total neglect of enforcement in the area of sports fishing. If the government wants a proper fishery on the west coast, it should realize this cannot be achieved using the same number of inspectors as in 1948. As well, changes will have to be made in the regulations which will ensure the continued growth of the tourism industry in the province.
I had four other points to make, Mr. Speaker, but I see that I will not have time so I will go over a couple of them briefly and quickly. The first is the economic insensitivity of this government. British Columbia has a great opportunity to develop its north-eastern area through the B.C. coal agreement. The amount of money involved is staggering and the benefits to Canada could be colossal. These include a 72-mile railroad costing $350 million. Through the National Harbours Board and the CNR the line to Prince Rupert would be upgraded at a cost of $50 million and $80 million worth of new rolling stock would be purchased. A new coal loading port would cost $70 million. Over 15 years the shipment value of the coal is expected to reach $7.04 billion. Those are some of

the benefits. I cannot agree with my friends to my left who are afraid to sell a little coal. British Columbia has thousands of years of coal stocks, mountains of it. The development of the railway would open up a new portion of the province and allow ancillary mines and industries to develop through the area. Yet there are arguments, there is nit-picking, niggardliness rather than a push to make the deal and get the job done. The taxation accruing to the federal government from this deal would more than meet any up front money the government of British Columbia is seeking.
Early this afternoon an hon. member gave some figures for research and development in this country which illustrate how backward we are in this area. Out of a population of 23 million, 21,519 people are engaged in research and development. This must make us the laughing stock of the world. It is almost criminal that a government could avoid thinking about this, could avoid changing the situation.
This government spent all its time worrying about something the country is not worried about, that the country is not even thinking about. It forces us to do the same and ignores the real problems in the country, such as creation of more jobs.
I should like to see the government produce an industrial strategy for Canada, show concern for the small independent businessman, introduce a program to increase jobs and productivity, a program to bring in lower interest rates, a program to reduce inflation. The failure of this country and this government to deal with the key issues which concern the people brings shame on all who sit on the benches opposite. Mr. Speaker, this motion should be passed.
